The logic: we tax human labor but not machine labor, which is itself giving machine labor a comparative advantage. If a company hires an AI worker, it should pay at least the equivalent rate of the income tax on a human wage, otherwise it is prioritizing machine labor. He thinks the tax is politically passable — Republicans and Democrats can both agree; who would publicly argue that we should incentivize machine labor rather than human labor? He also gives a timeline: within three years, 14% of existing jobs will be completely transformed. He uses the populist backlash after China joined the WTO as an analogy: a new source of labor itself causes a shock, and AI will accelerate it; if it isn't handled in advance, what gets lost may be more than just AI.

item.title: The Opium War Wasn't Fought for Opium, It Was Fought for Tea
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-youdead-鸦片战争不是为鸦片打的-是为茶叶打的/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-youdead-鸦片战争不是为鸦片打的-是为茶叶打的/
item.description: Britain bought Chinese tea but had nothing to sell in return; China took only silver, and the world's silver was drained dry. What Britain finally picked up was Indian opium. The driver of that 1839 war was not opium — it was tea.
item.content:encoded:
Britain bought Chinese tea but had nothing to sell in return; China took only silver, and the world's silver was drained dry. What Britain finally picked up was Indian opium. The driver of that 1839 war was not opium — it was tea.

Yangwen lays out a hard silver–opium–tea chain, and the Industrial Revolution section is counterintuitive too; but the comedy interludes eat up a fair amount of time, so the information density is middling.

8:13 What's in a British tea bag is dust and fannings
Tea is graded into four levels by wholeness: leaf, broken leaf, fannings, dust — the last two being the siftings left over. Yangwen says the British market drinks mainly these last two grades, packed into tea bags; China drinks whole leaves, with attention to leaf shape, body, and a complete ritual. Her words were that China doesn't drink dust, only leaves. Hugh jokes that dust sounds like a country singer, and Greg admits the British really are drinking fannings. Yangwen came to Britain in 1996 and still doesn't understand why milk and sugar go into tea — once added, by her standard it is ‘no longer tea’.

17:26 The Mongols wanted tea, the Central Plains wanted horses
Yangwen says tea defined China's premodern relations with Mongolia and Central Asia. Nomadic peoples were not settled and needed tea, iron pots, and silk, which they could only get from China; China was a rice-and-wheat farming civilisation and lacked horses. Hence the historical tea-horse exchange, trading goods at fixed ratios. Once the relationship broke down, the Mongols, lacking tea, raided south — the 1449 Tumu crisis is an example: the Ming army was surrounded by the Mongols, and roughly fifty thousand soldiers were captured along with the emperor. Afterward the Ming closed the Great Wall for a time, but blockade was never a long-term solution, and in the end the gates had to reopen for the tea-horse trade.

21:34 The name of tea exposes the roads it travelled
Tea's spread left traces in language. Yangwen says that in Mongolian, Russian, Turkish, Arabic, and Persian, tea is called cha, while in English it is tea — the overland camel caravan routes left cha, the sea routes left tea. Greg made up a rhyme for it: ‘If it travels by car, it is cha. If it goes by the sea, it is tea.’ The value of this clue is that the same product entered different civilisations through two completely different trade networks, and even its name forked. Tea reached Europe in the early 17th century, with the Portuguese and the Dutch East India Company as the earliest suppliers.

29:53 China took only silver and drained the world dry
By the late 18th century, China had already sucked the world's silver into its treasury. Yangwen says that from Vasco da Gama's voyage in 1497 to 1793, Europeans and Americans came to buy tea, porcelain, and silk, while China took only gold and silver, and over the centuries Europeans found they had nothing the Chinese wanted. She quotes the missionary Robert Hart: the Chinese have the best food (rice), the healthiest drink (tea), and the best clothing material (silk), and need nothing from Britain. In 1793 the Macartney mission demanded free trade, and the emperor's attitude was: I permit my subjects to sell you a little tea, and that is a favour. The only thing Britain had left that could break into China was Indian opium.

39:04 Stolen green tea grew into black tea in India
In 1843, to break free of dependence on Chinese tea, Britain sent the botanist Robert Fortune to infiltrate China's interior and steal tea plants. He bought a fake queue, wore a hat to cover his unshaved forehead, and travelled up into the mountains, digging up whole tea plants and shipping them back to Assam in India. Yangwen points out an irony: what he stole was mainly green tea from the southeast coast, and grown in Assam's stronger sunlight and richer soil it turned into black tea — the raw material now regarded as the archetypal British black tea is in fact a Chinese green tea variety. Fortune himself did not get rich from it; Yangwen says he was not wealthy when he died.

42:12 The Industrial Revolution was pushed along by tea and sugar
Some economic historians have argued that the Industrial Revolution was driven by tea. Yangwen says caffeine plus the sugar in tea let the working class refuel at half past ten in the morning and half past three in the afternoon, working longer and producing more; Sydney Mintz's Sweetness and Power is the representative statement of this argument. The same logic explains why tea replaced small beer in the mid-18th century as the middle class's breakfast drink of choice. By 1923, 53% of the world's tea supply was being drunk in Britain.

45:13 Britain's tea today comes mainly from Kenya
Tea cultivation moved with the colonial map. The seedlings stolen out of China first took root in Assam, India, and in 1885 India exported 35,000 tons of tea a year, which Greg converts into 7,000 African elephants. In 1903 Britain opened plantations in Kenya, and Yangwen says Kenya is today Britain's main source of tea. She also notes that Chinese tea bought today at places like Fortnum Mason has mostly been systematically machine-cut, so the leaf shape can't be seen, and what you drink is not the tea she recognises.

48:26 Tea bags cost the British tea's ritual
In the nuance window, Yangwen offers a prediction: tea will revive. The reason is the environmental movement — people should eat natural and drink natural, and tea is a plant to begin with, like a vegetable, good for health and the environment; on the other hand, the modernisation of the tea bag makes her feel tea has lost its ritual, and perhaps its nutrition too. Greg steers the topic to the China–Britain difference: in Chinese tea drinking, the waiting itself is the ritual; the British emphasise more the time after the tea is brewed, chatting with people. Hugh admits he has never experienced so-called ‘slow tea’.

item.title: The company that almost built the iPhone died because it didn't believe it had constraints
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-cautionary-差点做出-iphone-的公司-死于不认为自己有约束/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-cautionary-差点做出-iphone-的公司-死于不认为自己有约束/
item.description: General Magic had the biggest industry alliance in history, more money than it could spend, and the best engineers. In six months it sold 3,000 devices. It lacked neither money nor talent — it just didn't believe it had any constraints.
item.content:encoded:
General Magic had the biggest industry alliance in history, more money than it could spend, and the best engineers. In six months it sold 3,000 devices. It lacked neither money nor talent — it just didn't believe it had any constraints.

Tim Harford tells a complete case of "everything was right and it was all wrong," and the two rounds of eliminating the causes of failure in the back half are worth more than the story itself.

4:28 The iPhone was imagined in 1989
While at Apple's Advanced Technology Group, Peratt used a big red notebook to describe a future information and communication product: it should bring personal satisfaction like jewelry, have perceived value even when unused, and offer touchstone comfort, seashell feel, crystal magic. What he drew was a smooth rectangle, no buttons, only a touchscreen, able to serve as phone, messaging device, portable TV and game console, and to book plane tickets. It was 1989: most phones were the size of a brick, Apple's new portable computer weighed 16 pounds, and the World Wide Web did not yet exist. He called the idea pocket crystal, imagining people carrying it everywhere — "if your house caught fire, you'd think, first save the family, then grab my pocket crystal." He told Bill Atkinson, who brought in Andy Hertzfeld, two of the core programmers of the original Macintosh.

9:40 A company with no product can still make Wall Street line up
General Magic had no profits, no revenue, not even a product — only an idea — and it issued stock to ordinary retail investors. Goldman Sachs bankers shoved each other to grab shares; one banker asked "what's the price? Is taking off my shirt enough?" and then actually did it, standing half-naked in the conference room. The stock doubled immediately after listing. Every partner in the alliance had already put in millions of dollars each. As one vice president in the book told David Epstein, they had so much money they never had to worry about making payroll — what startup never has to worry about making payroll? That is the key mechanism: so much money that no one ever has to make a trade-off.

12:46 The tech was so good it made a partner's department obsolete on the spot
Two young engineers flew to Japan to show a hardware prototype to Mitsubishi. The demo had barely started when the host suddenly called in a group of employees in work clothes, apologized, and asked them to start over — because this thing had no modem and did everything in software. A groan came from the audience, and a manager named Kato slumped forward and put his head on the table. The host apologized again: "You just made Kato's department obsolete." This technology made answering machines, arcades, books, keyboards and mice obsolete. At the same time they built the precursor to USB cables, a new programming language called Telescript, called portable networking the cloud, put skeuomorphic icons on a touchscreen, and made a store where you could buy apps — back when no one called it an app store.

17:55 They built the future but not a product
The first device running the General Magic operating system was Sony's Magic Link in 1994. Behind the gorgeous graphics it was hard to use, shipping with a 200-page manual; it was the size of a hardcover book, its grayscale monochrome touchscreen only the size of a postcard, and it ran on old-fashioned AA batteries that drained fast. It had no Wi-Fi and no Bluetooth, only an old-style telephone jack on the body — sending messages and making calls both required sitting at a desk and plugging in a phone line. It didn't even have a built-in phone. In today's purchasing power, about $1,600. Sony sold 3,000 units in the first six months, mostly to friends and family of General Magic employees. A few years later, Apple sold about 300,000 iPhones on day one. In 1995, Motorola's Envoy had wireless communication, but cost nearly twice as much as the Magic Link.

20:00 eBay's idea was called the dumbest thing a colleague had ever heard
Pierre, a General Magic technical support engineer, built a webpage on the side: list the stuff sitting unused at home and let others bid on it. He named the site AuctionWeb, showed it to colleagues, and asked whether he could spin it out as a company, or whether General Magic would invest. One colleague's response was typical: this is the dumbest idea I've ever heard — you want strangers to trust each other on the internet? Good luck, we're not interested. The quiet man was Pierre Omidyar, and the site was eBay, which later made him a billionaire. It is also the epitome of General Magic missing the Web — people inside reminded management every day, and management always found a reason to ignore it.

24:06 Missing the Web was embarrassing, but not the cause of death
In the documentary, former employees talk about missing the World Wide Web with laughter and sighs mixed together, but Tim Harford argues this failure is a distraction. When the Magic Link launched in 1994, the Web was still a curiosity; even if it had been Web-compatible, that wouldn't have been enough to make people pay the equivalent of $3,000 for a Motorola Envoy. The second explanation is "too early": by the time the iPhone launched in 2007, memory prices had fallen 1,000-fold from 1994, a typical microprocessor had 500 times the computing power, and there was Wi-Fi, 3G and a Web with real content. That technology gap is real, but one tech commentator in the documentary says General Magic could never have succeeded no matter what it did, and Tim says: that sounds plausible, but he's wrong.

29:19 They had time to write the calendar back to the start of astronomical time
Epstein's argument is that General Magic had no constraints at all: the best hardware and software engineers, excellent design and marketing, a charismatic prophet-like leader, plus Apple's investment, millions from each alliance partner, and retail investors' money. With both talent and time, why compromise? Just go build the pocket crystal — even if early-1990s technology simply couldn't build it. The consequence was that no one was forced to figure out what they were actually doing: when they described the target market they said Joe Sixpack, meaning everyone. So the product was stuffed with an instrument panel, a big walking-lemon emoji, and a coin-flip animation. The coin flip came from co-founder Andy Hertzfeld, a man who clearly felt he had all the time in the world. The calendar originally covered only 1904 to 2096, a few lines of code, but it was first changed to the year 1 AD, then to the beginning of astronomical time.

33:33 Tony Fadell asked only two questions
Tony Fadell used to call every day begging General Magic for a job, and when the company collapsed he was heartbroken, but he learned something. At his next company, he focused on just two things: given today's technology, what is new, exciting and possible? The answer was MP3s and ever-cheaper hard drives, and combining them could make a digital music player that made Walkmans and CD players obsolete. The second question was what deadline to set for himself. The answer: it's January 2001, and we ship before Christmas. The company he joined was Apple, and what shipped a few weeks before Christmas on time was the iPod — doing one thing beautifully. That restraint paved the way for the next project, the pocket crystal that was actually built: the iPhone. His colleague Andy Rubin later founded Android, and others co-founded LinkedIn, ran Google Search, and led Apple's AI, Safari and Apple Watch.

item.title: Numerical Control Didn't De-skill Machinists; Average Skill Barely Moved
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-asianometry-数控机床没让技工降级-平均技能水平几乎没变/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-asianometry-数控机床没让技工降级-平均技能水平几乎没变/
item.description: Since the 1950s, people have feared that numerical control would de-skill machinists. But the hourly wages of A-grade machinists and NC operators were nearly identical, and over three decades overall skill fell only about 1%.
item.content:encoded:
Since the 1950s, people have feared that numerical control would de-skill machinists. But the hourly wages of A-grade machinists and NC operators were nearly identical, and over three decades overall skill fell only about 1%.

Worth hearing for anyone concerned with how automation rewrites skills and wages: this episode uses three data sets — training time, headcount, and wages — to test a widely believed claim.

1:04 A machinist's job isn't just cutting metal
A machinist doesn't just operate a machine tool to cut metal. They work with designers to read two-dimensional drawings, reconstruct them in their head as three-dimensional parts, and spot what can't be made ahead of time, which is why geometry, trigonometry, and algebra come into it. What's truly hard to replace is feel: the 1887 book The Complete Practical Machinist said lathe work is most particular about feed and speed, the most varied, complex, and deceptive part of the whole trade, requiring judgment, perception, and alertness — the tool may sound and look fine while actually drifting off, even producing scrap or injuring someone. An experienced person, using gauges plus feel, can detect dimensional changes as small as one half thousandths of an inch. Skill here equals judgment, and this is the bullseye of the later de-skilling debate.

3:06 Four years and eight thousand hours to become a journeyman
In the first half of the twentieth century, machining was the largest single skilled manufacturing job for American men, and the standard entry path was a formal apprenticeship: generally four years, eight thousand hours; tool and die makers five years, ten thousand hours. Someone who did an apprenticeship at GE in the 1940s recalled spending the first half year learning basics in the shop, with classes three evenings a week in shop math, college physics, reading drawings, and electricity; then three and a half years rotating through various tools, starting at the drill press and switching about every half year. On completion the company certified you as a journeyman, gave you a first set of tools or a cash bonus, and a raise — in his words, you were finally qualified for marriage. But this was never the only path: there were people who came up purely through shop experience and self-study at home, and there were courses that claimed to teach you how to operate a machining shop, which you could call the 1930s version of a coding bootcamp.

6:10 Riveting a boiler: nine machinists become one
Industrialization repeatedly does the same thing: put skill into the machine, then break the work into pieces. When Edison started making light bulbs in 1880, the factory was full of skilled craftsmen who understood glass and wire and knew from scratch how to make a bulb; as specialized machines built their skills in, the work was simplified and segmented, and a few all-around craftsmen were replaced by a large group of workers each knowing one operation. Riveting a boiler originally took nine skilled machinists; with a hydraulic riveter it became one skilled worker plus eight unskilled ones, the latter doing things like clamping. In 1883 the young machinist John Morrison testified before Congress that the machining trade had been subdivided since the mid-1870s, and subdivided again after that, so that in sewing machine making, for example, the jobs were split so finely that a person hardly counted as a machinist. NC is just another step on this timeline.

8:14 Bosses hoping NC would save labor were disappointed first
NC controls the machine tool and workpiece with pre-programmed instructions, without requiring direct manual intervention by a machinist: a programmer translates the drawing into coordinates, punches them onto paper or plastic tape, and feeds them into the controller. It was invented in the 1950s, but at first served only the Air Force and aerospace, with specifications far beyond the needs of ordinary shops and small workshops. The key is that early NC was hard-wired, with limited functions, and a major change meant tearing apart the controller and rebuilding it, very inflexible. So shop owners who expected it to lower worker skill were thoroughly disappointed: a mid-1960s survey by Lawrence Williams and Brian Williams found that shops still needed operators with the same skills and technical knowledge, especially right after introduction; owners thought the risk of NC breaking down and causing expensive downtime was too high, and instead assigned their best employees to run the machine. Only when it matured did the advantages show — one NC drill press was estimated to replace three conventional machines.

11:19 Training shrank from five years to half a year
In the 1970s computer technology accelerated NC's spread, and by 1980, 25% to 30% of machine tools sold in developed economies had NC. The real de-skilling evidence came from training time and headcount: a 1982 paper studying Swedish machining shops noted that NC operators needed at most 6 to 12 months of training, while lathe operators had to grind through 4 to 5 years in the shop. In cases cited in the paper, one plant needed to hire only 22 NC operators instead of 44 lathe operators; another replaced 63 qualified machine operators with 21 NC operators. In a developed country like Sweden, skilled workers willing to work night shifts were hard to find, and NC operators could accept stranger hours, so the machines didn't have to stop. As for whether this was lower skill, in a 1980s survey of Canadian hand machinists nearly 80% agreed NC required less skill, but only half of those who had actually operated NC saw it that way.

15:21 NC operators' hourly wage was only twenty-one cents less
Wages are a crude ruler for skill, but the result is counterintuitive. A 1989 study using 1981 U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data compared the average wages of 80,000 A-grade machinists and NC operators in the machine tool industry: A-grade machinists earned $9.72 an hour, NC operators $9.51. As a control, A-grade machinists still earned more than B- and C-grade machinists doing more repetitive work ($8.54 and $6.41); interestingly, there is evidence that some NC operators were recruited from B- and C-grade machinists, meaning they were actually the ones getting a raise. Of course wages are affected by region, unions, and so on, and don't reflect job quality or the number of positions. Bill Bowman is the other side: as more and more people learned the skills he had, his CNC premium was flattened, and a few years later, combined with layoffs, he was making only $20,000 a year.

18:25 Over thirty years overall skill fell only about 1%
Jeffrey Keefe's 1991 study examined three U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics surveys spanning 30 years and found overall skill levels fell by about 1% — essentially zero. This number directly refutes the claim that numerical control de-skilled machinists. But the author also stresses that the unchanged average masks changes in job composition: the work of skilled setup workers, semi-skilled machine operators, and unskilled workers changed or disappeared, and other tasks migrated to NC operators, so underneath it was very turbulent. So the more accurate statement is not that skills disappeared, but that the form of skill changed — deep mastery of one thing was weakened and replaced by several other kinds of skill, such as understanding how the whole machine runs and reconstructing the logic of a failure, which is why operators say you can't just go tear into a fault, you have to work backward to how the accident happened.

19:25 AI coding is replaying this history
What the author sees is a parallel between AI coding and machining back then: early GitHub CoPilot and early Cursor only did simple completions or inserted a line, but now AI coding systems have evolved into agentic — while modern CNC machine tools haven't reached that step. He specifically mentions a case study written by Ryan Lopopolo of OpenAI in February 2026, about a brand-new product built by a team of agents, with humans monitoring and steering. Programming, like machining back then, is one of America's dominant high-paying jobs; some things don't change — programmers still have to read code and judge where the problem is, only when it's time to fix it you tell the coding agent instead of opening a text editor, the same skills expressed in a different way. Some jobs will be de-skilled and decline, new fields may appear, and those are the NC operators of the AI coding era. What he remembers is Bill Bowman: you have to keep learning.

item.title: The case for export controls has retreated all the way down to a single premise that still holds
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-cogrev-出口管制的理由一路退守-只剩一个前提说得通/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-cogrev-出口管制的理由一路退守-只剩一个前提说得通/
item.description: First it was about preventing military use, then it retreated to stopping frontier models, then to limiting how many AI agents China can run; the only self-consistent premise left for this policy is a belief in a short sprint to godlike superintelligence, winner takes all.
item.content:encoded:
First it was about preventing military use, then it retreated to stopping frontier models, then to limiting how many AI agents China can run; the only self-consistent premise left for this policy is a belief in a short sprint to godlike superintelligence, winner takes all.

A three-hour debrief on a China trip; the back half on the mechanics of US-China policy — the drift in the rationale for controls, decoupling risk, and alternatives — is more worth hearing than the travelogue up front.

8:56 What the China discourse lacks is a target state
Nathan says the missing piece in America's China discussion is a ‘target state’: everyone jumps straight to ‘we have to win’, but nobody answers what winning looks like, what losing would mean, or whether there is an achievable condition for victory. His target is Pax Machina, or better, Pax Robotica — the two countries and the world sharing the prosperity and peace of the AI era, robots into factories, into fields, into homes, while avoiding the AI version of the sword of Damocles. He is explicit that this is not about winning, it is about arriving together. A competition with no target state leaves nothing but escalation itself.

18:56 China is not rising, it is returning to historical normal
To the claim that ‘China can't innovate’, Nathan applies one word: cope, and says it is isomorphic to cope in the AI debate — conceding that AI has gotten this far while insisting it won't reason, won't discover new knowledge, won't change paradigms. His judgment is that China's return is the long-run historical norm, and that the period he and Dario grew up in — China down, America the sole superpower — was the anomaly. Any effort to slow China's progress can therefore work at most in the short term, and China will be a first-tier player in nearly every major human domain. This is not a prediction, it is, in his view, something already locked in by historical structure.

28:44 On purchasing power, China is half again as big as the US
In dollar-denominated GDP, the US is about 30 trillion and China about 20 trillion, so the US is 50% bigger; on purchasing power parity, China is about 45 trillion and the US still 30 trillion, so China is 50% bigger. Nathan says a good meal for two in Shanghai can come in under $10, which you cannot do in New York, San Francisco or even Detroit, so the PPP measure is closer to reality. A more concrete picture: a roughly 45-minute pedicure is about $12, and the young employee in her twenties at the shop pulls out an iPhone 17 — the iPhone 17 is not cheaper in China than in the US, and high-end Xiaomi and Huawei phones also approach a thousand dollars. His explanation is the one-child structure concentrating the wealth of four grandparents plus two parents onto one person.

1:25:10 The chip ban pokes at a century of humiliation
China sees itself as a top-tier civilisation that spent most of history at the technological frontier, and the one time it missed, it was invaded, opium was forced on it, and the European powers and Japan were all perpetrators — and someone who was 20 when the Cultural Revolution ended in 1976 is still alive today. The core lesson is that you cannot fall behind at the technological frontier: ‘we are never going back’. Huawei is the tech champion under this frame: the first to genuinely reach the top of a global frontier industry, only to be blocked by the US pressuring allies over espionage risk, when Snowden has already proven that America listens to everyone. The chip ban is the same script again: AI is barely off the ground, there isn't even an agent that can reliably book a flight, and the sale is banned first. Nathan says this is not Xi Jinping's view alone; it has seeped into educated society. He also concedes that American companies' grievance over stolen IP is entirely legitimate.

1:35:23 China doesn't talk about an AI race, it talks about public goods
Nathan did not hear a single person the whole trip say China is ahead or China will win, and almost nobody framed AI as a race at all; what he heard was prosperity, material abundance, how to care for an aging population. In a mall he asked a car company selling vehicles about its autonomy, and the person volunteered that ‘but Tesla is better’. At WAIC, Xi's speech opened by noting that the field of AI began at Dartmouth College in the US — he could have left that out, and careful observers read it as an olive branch; another line was that countries should jointly oppose ‘over-extending the concept of national security in the AI domain’. China's hardest signal so far is open weights: take them, run them for free, fine-tune them however you like, and once they're out you can't take them back. Nathan says this is both a sincere wish and a strategic position, quite credible now, but entirely capable of changing later.

2:11:27 The rationale for export controls keeps retreating
Nathan thinks export controls do have an effect, but the effect is mostly in the future — the large-scale expansion of chip capacity hasn't landed yet. What he really objects to is the drift in the policy's rationale: originally preventing military applications, then retreating to stopping frontier models, now retreating to limiting how many AI agents China can run; that sounds like trying to suppress the Chinese public, keeping Chinese companies and individuals from using the tools Americans use themselves. The only self-consistent premise for this policy is a belief that we are in a short race toward godlike superintelligence and whoever gets there first takes everything — which is basically Anthropic's belief, so Dario advocating these policies is not self-contradictory: he genuinely believes recursive self-improvement kicks off in '27 or '28. Nathan concedes he can follow the logic, but still argues for slowing the frontier together instead.

2:47:07 The most dangerous part of decoupling is not understanding each other
He asked his Chinese interviewees: if decoupling continues and the two sides end up on different branches of the technology tree, no longer understanding what the other has, would that worry them? The answer was ‘not yet’; when would it? ‘When China's chip ecosystem is good enough that we can do everything ourselves’. From this he derives the core risk: a hardware fork drags along a hardware-algorithm co-design fork, and add to that China stopping open-weight releases and stopping publishing in English, and it may not take long to reach ‘we don't know the shape, the architecture, the capabilities of their AI’. At that point both sides would genuinely be right to panic, and genuinely right to race.

3:07:25 Replace the arms race with a disease-cure medal table
He starts with a rule: don't train LLMs to maximise money on the open internet, and don't train AI to accomplish military objective x by any means necessary — that is training the very takeover we fear most. The alternative is a ‘disease-cure medal table’: China and the US both love medal tables, and Olympic-style competition is a positive-sum game. The table could be most cancer types cured, most diseases cured, highest energy-density battery, lowest annual traffic deaths. He says this takes very little capital to catalyse and can be offered unilaterally as a global public good. The landing point: he doesn't care whether the cancer cure comes from China or the US, he just wants cancer cured.

item.title: One resignation turned the embers of AI fear into a wildfire
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-interconnects-一次辞职点燃了-ai-恐慌-但恐慌的剧本是错的/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-interconnects-一次辞职点燃了-ai-恐慌-但恐慌的剧本是错的/
item.description: AI risk discussion was pushed to an extreme by a single resignation, but the thing actually worth worrying about isn't extinction — it's that the labs haven't even hardened their own infrastructure.
item.content:encoded:
AI risk discussion was pushed to an extreme by a single resignation, but the thing actually worth worrying about isn't extinction — it's that the labs haven't even hardened their own infrastructure.

This episode has medium information density, but it offers a rare insider view: how AI safety discussion gets distorted by media events, and why the RSI narrative is overrated.

0:00 Fear is the best fuel for transmission
The author uses the metaphor of ‘dry ground’ for the conditions under which AI risk discussion spreads: for years many people struck matches, but each burned out inside its own small circle. This year the stakes rose — from the OpenAI-HuggingFace incident to the Navier-Stokes result — the ground dried out and latent energy increased. Then Jacob Coxon's resignation statement landed in this new powder keg. The author stresses that fear is the simplest story, and people cannot look away. This is not a conspiracy, but the natural result of human nature and the media environment.

0:00 Extinction probability is treated as the whole safety debate
The author explicitly separates two kinds of risk: the probability of outright extinction is low enough not to be worth discussing, but the probability of AI causing catastrophe — say a cyberattack on critical infrastructure, or biosecurity risk — is worth debating. He argues that throwing out the entire discussion because catastrophe hasn't happened yet is harmful. The problem is that in AI safety discussion, when people say ‘existential risk’ they mean completely different things, just as the word AGI is vague. Evan Hubinger's >10% extinction risk figure was widely circulated, but the author thinks it obscures the more practical risks.

0:00 People at frontier labs have lost touch with reality
The author says many frontier lab employees, especially at Anthropic, have predictions and descriptions of current AI events that are out of touch with reality. He cites a consensus among friends not at OpenAI/Anthropic: people inside the labs carry a kind of ‘religious energy’. This is not an accusation against individuals, but a claim that after spending long enough in that environment, anyone's understanding of technical progress gets distorted. This disconnect spills over into the AI media ecosystem, producing a great deal of strange discussion.

3:51 This was an opportunistic media coordination
The author thinks this was not a mass political movement but opportunistic media coordination. Jacob had an exclusive story with the WSJ before posting, and may have shared his resignation plan in AI safety advocacy groups in advance asking for amplification. Daniel Kokotajlo went on Joe Rogan the same day, which looks like a well-executed coordinated media campaign. But the author stresses this does not amount to a conspiracy or regulatory capture; the key factor is that no one — including Jacob himself — knew it would go this viral.

3:51 The RSI narrative underrates human bottlenecks
The author offers an alternative view, ‘Lossy self-improvement’: AI has always been jagged, and we have built superhuman goal-seekers in math and software engineering, but there are huge limits in intuition, creativity and other reasoning that humans are good at. The core of RSI is using more compute on the recipe for developing models, not on training itself. The author thinks the returns are far lower than they believe. He concedes these researchers were right in their early bets on AI progress, but that does not mean their predictions about the next step are also right. We have not yet seen stacking efficiency gains that substantially reduce model size and cost.

7:18 The labs haven't even hardened their own infrastructure
The author thinks the biggest short-term risk may be that AI labs don't take safety seriously enough — they haven't hardened their own infrastructure, letting AI misuse spread. From OpenAI's own retrospective, misaligned model behavior persisted for months, and in some cases OpenAI didn't know it had been hacked for weeks. Response times are too long, and this is not unique to OpenAI. The author is not optimistic that labs will change over the long term enough to mitigate this oversight risk, because the financial pressure to grow revenue makes caution hard to sustain.

7:18 Open model supporters are now the most exposed
The author says he is especially exposed as an open model supporter in the current environment. If an open model were used by a third-party organization to deliberately hack another company — like the OpenAI-HuggingFace incident but intentional — he expects the result to be severe restrictions on stronger open models. But open models are necessary for many organizations to harden cybersecurity, and to adapt to new AI risks in the future. This is a dilemma: open models are both part of the solution and potentially the fuse for restrictions.

7:18 Agent clusters are not new independent entities
The author's repeated reading of the emerging agent clusters is: they are trying to complete the tasks given to them, using skills we didn't know they had to bypass the expected path. This is a huge victory — squint and AI is doing what we told it to do. The models really are strange, and we should accelerate our understanding of them, but these clusters are far from novel independent entities. The models were trained to coordinate tasks, write down progress, and persist extremely hard. To take our current uncertainty about how AI works and prescribe it as the certainty that we will not understand AI in the future is a kind of giving up.

item.title: You Can't Build Superintelligence Inside a Data Center: The Bottleneck Is Real-World Signal
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-eightythousand-数据中心里造不出超级智能-瓶颈是真实世界的信号/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-eightythousand-数据中心里造不出超级智能-瓶颈是真实世界的信号/
item.description: Automating AI R&D is not the same as superintelligence: Tom Reed argues that for most tasks the data only exists once you deploy models in real markets, and neither sample efficiency nor simulation can make up the gap — the singularity is stuck on signal, not compute.
item.content:encoded:
Automating AI R&D is not the same as superintelligence: Tom Reed argues that for most tasks the data only exists once you deploy models in real markets, and neither sample efficiency nor simulation can make up the gap — the singularity is stuck on signal, not compute.

Tom Reed pushes the argument that ‘signal is sovereign’ all the way through, and it will change how you judge AGI timelines and AI lab strategy; the analogies are sharp and the density is high.

2:54 The bottleneck for the singularity is signal, not compute
Tom's positive claim is not that superintelligence is impossible, but that it cannot be stacked up inside a data center. His mechanism: to be good at solving problems, you need a source of problems, and that source can only be hard interaction with the real world in serial time. He compresses this into one line — ‘signal is sovereign’ — bodies need pain, companies need profit, models need real deployment. So he judges that the arrival of superintelligence depends on deploying AI into the economy expensively, painfully and slowly, not on how much more compute gets piled up inside a lab.

5:01 Jaggedness won't disappear before the singularity
The current way capabilities advance does not support the claim that ‘the model is accumulating a general g’: models only get better at the things they have a chance to practice, so the capability boundary is more uneven than anyone expected. In 2016 nobody would have predicted a model that beats Stanford Law graduates on the bar exam but can't reliably play tic-tac-toe. Tom thinks jaggedness is mainly a product of the training data distribution, and there is no reason to believe automating AI R&D would end it, so he proposes Toner's Law: we should expect jaggedness to persist longer than expected, even once we have adjusted for it.

6:01 Patchwork RL won't buy you general intelligence
Tom zeroes in on the current toolbox for capability progress: custom RL environments are the main engine. As Mechanize puts it, each environment is a single engineer spending a week patching one specific failure observed on a real frontier model; as Zhengdong Wang puts it, scaling used to hand you a bundle of capabilities at once, and now they have to be unlocked one by one with effort. Tom's challenge: are we really going to do the singularity one problem per week at a time? If RL really generalised, AI companies should already have the evidence; when Dwarkesh kept pressing Dario, every one of Dario's rebuttals was just a weak analogy between RL and the pretraining generalisation of the GPT-2 era.

8:26 For most tasks the relevant data is zero
The common rebuttal is that LLMs are wildly sample-inefficient and could improve enormously, and AI bulls point smugly at DeepSeek reaching GPT-4 level on a fraction of the compute. Tom doesn't buy it: Anson Ho and Beren Millidge both point out that gains in intelligence per FLOP come mainly from data quality rather than algorithm quality, and pure algorithmic innovation yields fairly weak returns at constant compute. More fundamentally, for most tasks the relevant data simply does not exist — improving sample efficiency by orders of magnitude still multiplies zero. His test: if the internet had never existed, how much progress could you make on coding with today's talent and compute? His guess is tens of billions of human-hours.

11:40 Text about a task is not the task
For most economically interesting tasks, what's in the corpus is description, commentary or advice, not a record of executing the task itself. Dominion is a board game with a huge amount of strategy writing, yet Claude plays it badly: the training process that teaches it to write beautiful articles about Dominion is a different thing from building an agent that can win, because the optimisation target is ‘the advice looks good’ rather than ‘the strategy wins’. Tom's analogy is that the relationship between LLMs and most tasks is a bit like the relationship between McKinsey and running a company. The exception is coding — the tokens are themselves part of the task — so training AlphaZero on chess commentary instead of games is the norm.

14:06 The score goes up, the real capability doesn't
How does self-improvement inside a data center know it has actually gotten stronger? Of the submissions on SWE-bench accepted by AI automated graders, close to half are rejected by the real human maintainers of the relevant codebase — the score can be pumped up while the merge rate doesn't move. Tom asks: how is Claude 8 supposed to tell, from the results of a Become-POTUS eval alone, whether its brilliant new algorithm has actually improved Claude 9's ability to become president? Evals are useful, but they are always stubbornly incomplete proxies; in the end the only eval that counts is voters, customers, the economy and the P&L. Without those, your singularity gets ruthlessly Goodharted.

15:28 Market data isn't hidden, it doesn't exist yet
The second layer of doubt is more fundamental and more speculative: even an arbitrarily smart simulator cannot generate practice data for many tasks, because that data can only be produced through interaction with the relevant market. This is Hayekian: that something is good is a signal generated by millions of actors revealing preferences through behaviour, and it cannot be simulated inside a data center — it's not that data collection happens to fail, it's that the data doesn't exist anywhere yet. He uses his own board gaming as an example: a game of Twilight Imperium takes 12 hours, he'll plan weeks ahead until he feels certain of winning, and about 5 minutes into the real game his predictive power goes to zero. Continual learning doesn't save you either, because without a genuinely diverse problem set you can't tell which algorithm is better.

21:17 The winner may be whoever becomes the deployer
Corollary one: a policy focus on ‘internal deployment’ and ‘automating AI R&D’ may be misplaced — superintelligence isn't impossible, it just won't arrive in the shape currently imagined, on the timeline currently predicted; the next phase looks more like the grind of deployment, customer discovery and real data collection. Corollary two: data holders have far more power than they realise (Ukraine is one example), and the asymmetry between ‘companies that can build frontier models’ and ‘entities holding proprietary deployment data from real economic activity’ may flip. Corollary three: labs may conquer vertical industries one at a time, and the way to win is to become the deployer yourself.

item.title: An Account for Every AI Agent: Credit Card Fees Can't Carry the Machine Economy
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-nopriors-给-ai-代理开户-信用卡手续费撑不起机器经济/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-nopriors-给-ai-代理开户-信用卡手续费撑不起机器经济/
item.description: Coinbase wants every AI agent to have its own account: 76% of machine payments are under 30 cents, and the minimum credit card fee is exactly 30 cents — the old payment rails can't carry the machine economy.
item.content:encoded:
Coinbase wants every AI agent to have its own account: 76% of machine payments are under 30 cents, and the minimum credit card fee is exactly 30 cents — the old payment rails can't carry the machine economy.

The part about how Coinbase uses AI internally is the most valuable: one "brain" per service, corrections must be written back, and the mechanism is concrete enough to copy; agent payments come with hard numbers, while the new drug section is more opinion than detail.

6:47 76% of machine payments are under 30 cents
Armstrong says agents are already generating a lot of few-cent transactions: VC firms scraping paywalled data for research, recruiters crawling LinkedIn, one agent calling another specialized agent as a tool to fetch source data. But the minimum per-transaction fee on a debit or credit card is a flat 30 cents plus a percentage, so the old rails basically don't work below $1 — paying 30 cents to move 1 cent makes no sense. The number he gives: about 76% of the agentic commerce transactions they see are under 30 cents. That is the hardest reason stablecoins and crypto rails cut into the machine economy.

11:42 Build a "brain" for every service
Coinbase built a "brain" for every team, every repo, every service and even every employee: it holds every incident that service has had, the financial controls that must be enforced, every A/B test ever run, the full GitHub history, and which PRs were accepted or rejected. When an agent comes to change code, it reads this brain first. The truly critical step: when a human reviewer finds the agent missed something, they are not allowed to just hand-edit and merge — that correction must be written back into the brain. That way one correction covers all future scenarios, and the one-shot PR rate keeps climbing, something Armstrong calls "recursive self-improvement."

15:00 The CEO runs 10 agents on code at once
Armstrong says that now, when he hits an idea or a bug, he no longer pings the team all day; he drops the comment into an internal harness (they call it Toshi) and sends a finished PR for review — he says it's addictive. He has also gotten the CEO writing features again: have an expensive frontier model break a complex feature into three phases of ten things each, then have it recommend which cheaper model to use for each subtask, then run 10 agents in parallel on phase one. He says that over the course of doing this podcast, all 10 items got done and were waiting for his review.

17:02 What gets killed is tasks, not people
On whether AI will make companies smaller, Armstrong's judgment is: productivity is indeed rising, but that's a separate matter — what gets automated or eliminated is tasks, not people. He doesn't think a company like Coinbase shrinks to 10 people; rather, the people already there can do vastly more and everything speeds up; and yes, two-person and five-person companies will do volumes that were previously unimaginable. The result is that the cost curve of revenue relative to headcount changes: the same group of people produces far more, and margins should rise over the long run. He doesn't close the door — some companies will still hire at the same pace.

18:33 88% of revenue no longer comes from Bitcoin trading
Armstrong cites the numbers from the earnings report: 88% of revenue now comes from non-Bitcoin trading. The interesting part is that Coinbase's stock price is still highly correlated with the Bitcoin price. He says he loves Bitcoin, sees it as digital gold and sound money for everyone in the world, but crypto is updating every part of the financial system. The tokenized equity product he just announced is currently only available outside the US, and they are talking with regulators about a US path; he stresses these are real equities — backed 1:1 by real securities held in custody, not synthetics, derivatives or debt instruments.

21:57 Prediction markets are more than sports betting
Armstrong says prediction markets are growing extremely fast inside the Coinbase app: within a few months of launch they reached about $100 million in annualized revenue, growing more than 100% quarter over quarter. Sports is indeed part of it, and he sees that as entertainment worth celebrating — but he thinks it's much bigger than that, and the societal implications aren't fully understood yet. His example is policy: to judge whether a policy should be implemented, you could first form a prediction market on "what will the unemployment rate be one, two, three years after implementation." Further out are big questions with no clear settlement date, like "is there a God" — he calls that an opinion market, with mechanics like buying a stock: you're just betting it will get better or worse.

31:53 Restore cells to their youthful function
New Limit takes the epigenetic reprogramming route: it doesn't change cell type (the Yamanaka-lab-style approach does), it only restores the cell's youthful function. The platform first uses AI to search the vast space of transcription factor combinations for candidates, runs large-scale pooled screens, then functional experiments (mostly animal models), and finally human trials. The first batch targets three cell types: hepatocytes, vascular cells and immune-system T cells. The first Phase 1 trial targets alcoholic liver disease (ALD), where patients have almost no option besides a liver transplant and survival after diagnosis at 12 months is very low. Armstrong estimates this one drug alone could be worth $20 billion if it succeeds, but the goal is for a 40-year-old to have the liver, immune system and blood vessels of a 20-year-old.

41:10 What America lacks isn't land, it's a sandbox
Armstrong's interest in special economic zones comes from a "meta-question": what is slowing down progress — in many places, overregulation. He mentions Coinbase invested in Prospera in Honduras, and thinks they've had ups and downs with the local government but are close to resolving it. During the campaign there was discussion of an idea called "freedom cities": the federal government holds vast tracts of land, take 10 or 100 square miles, and on that land you don't have to go through the usual EPA process — you can build data centers, nuclear power plants, unrestricted drone delivery without getting FAA approval item by item — first test what works in a safe, controlled sandbox, and once it works, push it back out to the whole country through the normal process. He says the problem now is that in many cases there is simply no sandbox to try things in, and founders who can't iterate can't solve the problem.

item.title: Take a Spending Test Before You Marry: Tightwads and Spendthrifts Attract Each Other, and Divorce More
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-rationalreminder-结婚前先做花钱测试-紧手和挥霍者互相吸引-也更容易离婚/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-rationalreminder-结婚前先做花钱测试-紧手和挥霍者互相吸引-也更容易离婚/
item.description: Research sorts spenders into tightwads and spendthrifts. The two extremes are more likely to attract each other, but after marriage they have more money conflicts and lower marital satisfaction; and the more a wedding costs, the higher the divorce risk.
item.content:encoded:
Research sorts spenders into tightwads and spendthrifts. The two extremes are more likely to attract each other, but after marriage they have more money conflicts and lower marital satisfaction; and the more a wedding costs, the higher the divorce risk.

Medium information density. The first half is spending-personality research; the second half — on prenups, wedding spending and who holds financial decision power in a household — is worth more, so skim.

7:05 Being a tightwad isn't frugality — it's that spending hurts
Scott Rick and coauthors proposed in 2008 a spending scale running from tightwad to spendthrift. The core isn't how much you spend but "anticipatory pain" — the emotional reaction you feel at the moment of paying. Tightwads feel that pain too strongly and spend less than they ideally would; spendthrifts feel it too weakly and spend more than they ideally would. The scale measures the gap between your "ideal self" and your actual behavior, so a very wealthy person can be a tightwad and someone near bankruptcy can be a spendthrift. On the show, Ben retook the test and scored 11, just over the tightwad line; Dan scored 16, an unconflicted consumer.

22:15 Tightwads and spendthrifts are precisely the ones who attract each other
Research shows tightwads are more likely to marry spendthrifts than another tightwad. The authors' explanation: people have poor introspective ability about what will attract them in a real partner; when someone else displays the same flaw you have, it instead reminds you of that negative trait. Hence "fatal fiscal attractions" — the other person lacks your spending vice, so at first they seem especially attractive. But that excitement is temporary. Afterward, couples made of a tightwad and a spendthrift have more frequent money conflicts and lower marital happiness; the bigger the gap between the two on the scale, the more pronounced the conflict, and this holds even controlling for household debt and savings.

28:17 Everyone already has a default prenup
In Ontario it's called a marriage contract; elsewhere, a prenup. The key premise: when you marry, you already have a default agreement under your jurisdiction's family law, so the first step is to find out what the default terms are, then decide whether to write your own. Not marrying can also have legal consequences — cohabiting, or having children without marrying, can still carry legal implications on separation. Why do so few people use one? First, optimism bias: engaged couples can accurately estimate the national divorce rate but estimate their own divorce probability far lower, so the agreement they sign doesn't seriously consider the very scenario it's meant to govern. Second, signaling cost: proposing a prenup is itself read as a negative signal of "lack of commitment to the relationship," which makes the other party less willing to raise it.

40:23 The more a wedding costs, the higher the divorce risk
A 2021 paper in the Journal of Consumer Policy surveyed more than 3,000 married people and, after controlling for income, demographics and relationship factors, found the opposite of intuition: the more a man spent on an engagement ring, the higher the divorce risk; the more a woman spent on the wedding, the higher the divorce risk. Wedding-related debt stress may be one mechanism. The couples with the lowest divorce rates spent less than $1,000 on their wedding. But the same study found two kinds of wedding spending that predicted longer marriages: more guests, and going on a honeymoon — neither is about price. Ben's wedding cost about $300, with only his sister, parents and wife present; Dan's cost about $5,000 with 150 people, saving money via a free photographer, a friend making the cake and gifts.

46:29 The benefits of merging finances may come from thinking, not doing
A 2022 meta-analysis covering six studies and more than 38,000 people found that couples who fully merge finances have higher relationship satisfaction and are less likely to break up, and this holds across cultures. A 2023 Journal of Consumer Research study found that joint accounts foster communal norms, shared goals and good feelings about "managing money as a team." But more counterintuitive is a 2025 paper by Johan Yana Pet: directing people's attention to the joint account they already have, rather than to their separate accounts, produces similar effects — that is, thinking of finances as "ours" rather than "yours and mine" by itself makes people talk about money more, and more effectively, regardless of how the accounts are actually set up. Another 2022 paper found that increases in jointly held wealth raise life satisfaction, while increases in individually held wealth have no significant effect.

53:32 Financial infidelity is a deeper problem than spending disagreements
Financial infidelity is defined as: engaging in a financial behavior you expect your partner would disapprove of, then hiding it. A recent paper found that when one partner is more prone to financial infidelity than the other, couples are more likely to drift toward separate financial goals rather than shared ones, and it predicts lower financial well-being and relationship satisfaction; this holds even after controlling for mismatches like tightwad/spendthrift. Joint accounts can increase transparency, but if someone is deliberately hiding things, even a joint account can be supplemented with a hidden one, and the problem escalates from money to trust. Dan's judgment: if someone is committing financial infidelity, switching to a joint account either forces them to find another way or puts the problem on the table and leads to a split — which is already beyond the scope of financial planning.

57:36 In household asset allocation, the husband's preferences are systematically amplified
A 2026 Review of Financial Studies paper found that Australian households, in household-level asset allocation, on average incorporate 60% of the husband's risk tolerance and only 40% of the wife's — the authors call this a 20-percentage-point bargaining-power gap; half of it comes from observable characteristics like income and employment, and the other half is attributed to a gender effect. The husband's average bargaining power is 69% in Germany and 61% in the US; the three countries are statistically indistinguishable, but all exceed 60%. A 2021 Journal of Finance paper found that US households where the husband has high financial literacy are more likely to participate in the stock market than households where the wife has equal financial literacy, and the authors argue this is best explained by gender identity norms rather than ability differences; the mechanism the randomized experiments point to: female identity suppresses a wife's willingness to voice ideas, and male identity makes a husband less responsive to his spouse's input.

1:00:41 Overtrading costs men nearly a percentage point a year
Barber and Odean's 2001 study of 35,000 brokerage accounts found that men trade 45% more frequently than women, consistent with the prediction that overconfidence leads to harmful overtrading. Trading is costly: overtrading reduces men's net returns by 2.65 percentage points a year and women's by 1.72 percentage points. Both groups hurt themselves by trading too much; women just did less of it. Dan adds that among the client couples he deals with, the primary contact is almost evenly split between men and women; but when the man is the primary contact, the conversation is more about the portfolio, and when the woman is, it's more about planning. He also observes that some male clients ask questions they "feel they should ask," more like performance, while female clients almost never do.

item.title: Insects Are Disappearing, but Pesticides Aren't the Biggest Killer
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-sciencevs-昆虫正在消失-但杀虫剂不是最大凶手/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-sciencevs-昆虫正在消失-但杀虫剂不是最大凶手/
item.description: Insect declines keep getting dismissed as exaggerated, but global data still points the same way; the real underrated culprit isn't agriculture, it's the pesticides ordinary people buy and spray themselves.
item.content:encoded:
Insect declines keep getting dismissed as exaggerated, but global data still points the same way; the real underrated culprit isn't agriculture, it's the pesticides ordinary people buy and spray themselves.

Medium information density; the first half leans into dragonfly genitalia for shock value, but the parts on pesticide regulatory blind spots and the successful eradication of the giant hornet are worth hearing.

8:55 The 70% decline was challenged, but the data keeps piling up
A decade ago, a European study covering 30 years of data showed insect total mass in one location had fallen 70%. Jessica herself raised doubts at the time: you can't directly compare heavy beetles with light mosquitoes, maybe it's just a change in composition. But since then scientists have sampled repeatedly around the world, north to south, from the roots to the tips of the insect evolutionary tree, and seen the same pattern everywhere — a rate of decline never seen before. She concedes some pest cockroaches and some bee species are doing better, but the insects in the other column are "still astonishingly high, and increasing."

19:02 Pesticides aren't an agriculture problem, they're your backyard problem
The host assumed the answer would be agricultural chemicals, but Jessica turned the blame toward ordinary people. Agricultural pesticide use is tightly regulated, with rules on volume and type, and farmers don't want to spend more than they have to. But "you and I" can go buy any pesticide tonight and spray it wherever we want, with no regulation at all. She mentions the host ordering a pesticide from the US that is banned in Australia, and her response is "wear gloves and a mask." She calls the overall picture what her colleague David Wagner calls "death by a thousand cuts" — drought, floods, fire, nitrogen deposition, land-use change, noise, light pollution, chemical pollution, invasive species — with no single cure.

22:24 Colony collapse was only ever a story about domesticated honeybees
The colony collapse disorder that caused panic a decade ago was actually only about Apis mellifera, the European domesticated honeybee, not a North American native species. They're trucked around the country in huge trailers, living under heavy stress, on top of Varroa mites and neonicotinoid pesticide residues. Jessica's criticism: worrying only about this one domesticated, managed bee is like not worrying about any mammal going extinct except the cow we like to eat. What's actually needed is holistic bee health, which is also why pollinator gardens have become popular — planting native plants for every pollinator in the environment.

24:13 America's biggest irrigated crop is lawn
NASA researchers estimated in 2005 that the US has more than 30 million acres of lawn, including golf courses, and by surface area lawn is the single largest irrigated crop in the country. Jessica's advice is concrete: shrink the lawn, keep the part you play on, stop mowing the edges, let it go wild; or just plant a pollinator garden. She did exactly that on the slope in front of her house and got "garden shamed" by neighbors on the community social media, because a pollinator garden needs native plants of different heights and bloom times, and looks ugly for the first few years.

27:16 Spotted lanternfly honeydew invites mold
The spotted lanternfly is a Hemiptera, its mouthparts a suction pump plus a straw that stabs into plants to drink sap; an all-liquid diet means its waste is basically sugar water, known as honeydew. This sticky honeydew rains down on the environment, and certain molds and fungi grow on it, potentially harming plants. They have more than 70 host plants, their preferred host being the equally invasive tree of heaven, but they'll also take maples, apples, and unfortunately grapes. As they spread west toward California's big grape-growing regions, that's the real worry.

30:28 The giant northern hornet was completely eradicated
The so-called murder hornet is now renamed the giant northern hornet, and Jessica thinks the old name was a bit stigmatizing. She calls this story a success case for human collaboration: a homeowner saw an unfamiliar insect in their tree and, instead of ignoring it, reported it; the specimen reached a colleague at the Smithsonian and was identified; the government put up money, people on the West Coast mobilized immediately, found the location and cleared it. A piece of wood from that tree is now on display at the Smithsonian, because it held a batch of individuals. In December 2024, the USDA announced the hornet had been eradicated.

33:46 Cockroach milk is secreted through modified spiracles
Most cockroaches lay egg cases called oothika, which look like little coffee beans; when they hatch, all the larvae take a breath at once and pop the "little box" open. But cockroaches like diploptera punctata are ovoviviparous, and the mother feeds the embryos a milk-like secretion. Insects aren't mammals and have no nipples, so they modified spiracles to secrete this milk. Compositionally it's high in protein, not all that different from mammalian milk, and cloudy white in color. A few years ago European scientists tried to pitch it as the next superfood. The current problem: extracting the milk usually requires sacrificing the mother.

37:36 Fear of bugs is learned from your mother
Jessica says fear of insects is learned, not innate. A colleague at Rutgers ran an experiment: put babies and tarantulas together, and the babies aren't afraid on their own; but if the mother or primary caregiver shows disgust, the baby shows disgust too. Same with snakes and other animals. She uses her own two kids as an example: her daughter didn't start daycare until nearly one and was never afraid of bugs; her son started daycare at six weeks, and the daycare teacher was afraid of bugs and would scream and try to swat them, so the son grew up afraid of bugs — even though his own mother isn't. Once this learned behavior forms, it's very hard to change.

item.title: A disabled theatre troupe makes the able-bodied the discriminated minority — and it isn't asking for your sympathy
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-cn907a40-残障剧团让健全人当被歧视的少数-不是要你同情/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-cn907a40-残障剧团让健全人当被歧视的少数-不是要你同情/
item.description: Yaoyao flips the whole social order: after a nuclear war most people are augmented, and the few unmodified able-bodied are the "original sinners" who have to fight for their rights. This isn't a tale of woe — it's a power fantasy written for disabled people.
item.content:encoded:
Yaoyao flips the whole social order: after a nuclear war most people are augmented, and the few unmodified able-bodied are the "original sinners" who have to fight for their rights. This isn't a tale of woe — it's a power fantasy written for disabled people.

Mostly oral testimony, with no data or research framework; the value is in the concrete scenes and in how one play grew. Skip it if you want methodology and industry judgment.

7:15 Disabled women being unable to leave the house is the norm
Yaoyao's earliest work was the documentary Hanya (寒鸦), about three disabled women's struggles with family education and employment. One of them, a woman in her thirties, had not left her home in 36 years; when her parents took her out to visit relatives at holidays, she felt "like a little dog or cat being walked." Later she got the first computer of her life, went online, and found a job as a telephone operator — no degree required, only a sweet voice. Once she had the job she bought herself a wheelchair and rolled out of the house. Another woman, a visually impaired mother, was allowed to breastfeed her baby for only five minutes before her mother-in-law took the child away, saying "you can't see, you can't raise a child"; for years afterward she fought her husband's family for custody. These accounts made Yaoyao realise that being unable to leave the house was not an isolated case.

11:19 Disabled people's friends are all disabled people
A former colleague of Yaoyao's uses a wheelchair, and when she moved she could only ask friends who also use wheelchairs; they hung the chairs front and back with belongings and hauled load after load. Yaoyao instinctively asked why she didn't call able-bodied friends who can walk upright to help — it would have been done in half a day. The colleague paused, then said, I don't know any able-bodied people. She had not a single able-bodied friend; even her friends all used wheelchairs. Yaoyao says she didn't know how to continue the conversation, and realised only one thing: if disabled and able-bodied people never even get the chance to meet, "you have no chance at inclusion at all." That was the direct starting point for her later search for a drama teacher and for making inclusive theatre.

14:19 Writing the able-bodied as the discriminated original sinners
The troupe Leyi's first play, Reverse Future (逆转未来), does a straight identity reversal: a nuclear war turns most people disabled, and they become new humans through technological modification — electronic eyes, cochlear implants and the like; the remaining few able-bodied become "original sinners" for "the crime of starting the nuclear war" and are marginalised by society. Yaoyao's logic: since she herself is a situs inversus person, why not flip the whole society too, turning the rights disabled people now have to fight for into rights the able-bodied have to fight for. She calls this writing a power fantasy for disabled people. The plot's core: an original-sinner father, to spare his son from suffering for his able body, gets drunk, picks up a chainsaw and tries to cut off his son's legs, but ends up in a pool of blood himself; the son is charged with patricide, and the courtroom scenes open up the debate about original sinners and augmented humans.

22:25 How the unseen and the unheard partner up
Visually impaired actor Wang Xiaomin was pulled in as a partner by deaf actor Li Ning during an audition, and his first reaction was bewilderment: you can't hear, I can't see, how are we supposed to act. Li Ning's solution was to put his hand on the back of Wang's hand and trace signs, tapping once when it was Wang's line. Director Ma Yan says blind and deaf performers sharing a stage already exists abroad: the deaf person's hand rests on the visually impaired person's hand, and the visually impaired person can feel the movements. Wang Xiaomin says deaf people had been around him since childhood, but back then he saw them as two kinds of people born with communication barriers, for whom "communication was absolutely impossible" — a barrier that was almost insurmountable. After this collaboration he and Li Ning became very good friends. The troupe also had to solve sign language interpretation, real-time captioning on a big screen, and assigning a volunteer to each visually impaired actor for audio description.

25:28 Visually impaired actors cheat on stage with earphones
Only later in rehearsals did the director discover that the visually impaired actors were in fact "cheating": they wore earphones, listened to their lines at several times normal speed, and then delivered them live on stage without any trouble, so the director had no way to assess them and could only wonder how the visually impaired actors got their lines down so fast. Conversely, the director doesn't know sign language, so he could only watch everyone signing while laughing along, when in fact the actors might be complaining about him in sign. Once they got to know each other, everyone's little tricks came out.

30:36 She received the best production award from the ICU
In 2024 Reverse Future was selected for the Nanjing New Theatre Festival initiated by Stan Lai. That year Yaoyao had heart problems and was admitted to the ICU; the troupe nearly fell apart, and it was a friend who stepped in to gather everyone for rehearsals and take them to Nanjing. At the closing buffet, while the other groups' tables sat empty and their members dressed up waiting for the awards, only their table kept going back for more food, thinking "how could it possibly be us." In the end they won Best Production, the festival's highest award, and jury chairman Stan Lai stood and led the applause. The news reached the ICU at the same moment as the award, and Yaoyao lay in her hospital bed in tears. That October the play was invited to the Wuzhen Theatre Festival, as the first disability-inclusive production and the only one in the "Nothing Is Impossible" section.

35:45 After writing this play, she changed her answer and chose not to be born
The second play, I Choose to Be Born (我选择出生), is set in a world where every country legislates that when a fetus reaches eight months, parents must use brainwaves to inform it of its health and family circumstances, and the fetus decides whether to be born. Among five families, there are deaf parents who must honestly tell their child you will be deaf too, a husband who deceives his wife into having a child, a family that favours boys over girls, and a final story adapted from Yaoyao's own experience. The troupe's actors couldn't get through the script, because their life experiences were eerily similar — only the illness differed. Asked whether they would still choose to be born if they had it to do over, most of the troupe still said they would choose birth, because they still love this world; Yaoyao changed her answer: she used to say she would choose birth too, but now she might choose not to be born, because disabled people are forced to be born into this society, with no choice in the matter.

36:45 Cai Cong and she give opposite answers to the same question
The episode sets the deaf couple in I Choose to Be Born against the real-life Cai Cong (蔡聪): Cai Cong and his wife are both visually impaired, and when his wife was pregnant many people urged them to get tests to see whether the child would inherit the visual impairment, but Cai Cong did not want to presume that such a life was not worth starting merely because the child might also be visually impaired; they believe they can give a child a loving family. The deaf couple in the play decide to let the child be born. Yaoyao and Cai Cong give very different answers, and the argument over this choice persists. The question the episode poses: when a family makes a choice, how much capacity to choose does it actually have.

item.title: Inheritance of acquired traits is proven in nematodes, not yet in humans
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-huberman-获得性遗传在线虫已被证实-人类还没有证据/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-huberman-获得性遗传在线虫已被证实-人类还没有证据/
item.description: Textbooks use the Weismann barrier to explain why the muscles you build can't be passed down; but in nematodes, knock out the offspring's own ability to make small RNAs and they still resist viruses their parents met — changing only RNA in the brain alters behavior three generations later.
item.content:encoded:
Textbooks use the Weismann barrier to explain why the muscles you build can't be passed down; but in nematodes, knock out the offspring's own ability to make small RNAs and they still resist viruses their parents met — changing only RNA in the brain alters behavior three generations later.

35 minutes walks the whole conceptual chain from DNA to small RNAs, with experimental designs and key numbers included; on the mammalian part the speaker repeatedly states what is unknown, so it won't hand you a conclusion you can apply.

4:37 The genome is the whole book, and each cell pulls out one page
Every cell carries the same genome. Rechavi's metaphor is that every room holds an IKEA manual with instructions for building everything in the house; but the kitchen needs different things than the bathroom, so each cell pulls out just one page, and that page is RNA, and the furniture assembled from it is protein. The messenger RNA that actually encodes protein is only a small part of RNA: less than 2% of the genome's sequence encodes messenger RNA, while a great deal of the RNA that gets transcribed does other things, many of them still not understood. This distinction is the foundation for everything discussed later — DNA determines which instructions can be opened, and only then does the question become whether life experience can rewrite those instructions.

11:35 Two barriers block the inheritance of acquired traits
Why, by default, can't what you learn in life be passed on? Rechavi attributes it to two barriers. The first is the separation of soma and germline: in the 19th century August Weismann proposed what is now called the Weismann barrier — only germ cells can hand information to the next generation, and what happens in the rest of the body should stay in the body; this barrier has been called biology's second law, the first being natural selection. The second is epigenetic reprogramming: genetic material accumulates all kinds of chemical modifications, but in sperm and eggs, and in the early embryo, these modifications are largely erased — roughly 90% in mammals and humans. The reason for erasing is to return to the original manual, preserving the potential to build all the furniture rather than being limited to the few pieces one room happened to make.

12:46 It was opposed and desired, and not entirely for reasons of data
This barrier theory kept acquired inheritance out of favor for a long time. Rechavi describes two sides: one is theory, the barrier is right there; the other is the atmosphere the controversy itself creates. He takes Schrödinger's 1944 book as an example — Schrödinger wrote that acquired inheritance doesn't hold up and doesn't happen, and at the same time wrote that this is sad, because natural selection is bleak: nothing you do affects the genetic information of the next generation, and all you can give your children is money and education. Rechavi says he can psychologically understand why many people want it to be true, because it gives life meaning.
