But he doesn't push this into ‘because everyone wants to believe it, it has promise’; he only says RNA is a new lead, a candidate molecule that in recent years has come to the fore even in the mammalian field.

16:20 Nematodes can run hundreds of generations in one PhD
Why should you trust nematodes? The conditions Rechavi lists are concrete: a C. elegans is always 959 cells, 302 of them neurons, and since the 1980s it has had a complete connectome, like a subway map marking who talks to whom; the body is transparent, so you can watch neurons fire directly, and you can switch genes on and off with optogenetics; it was the first animal to have its genome sequenced, earlier than humans; each mother produces about 250 nearly genetically identical offspring, kept in a dish eating bacteria, in a highly controlled environment where nature and nurture can be separated; generation time is 3 days, so one PhD can run through hundreds of generations of nematodes. Under these conditions, he says, the inheritance of acquired traits in nematodes already has very clear, indisputable evidence, and almost no one in the epigenetics field disputes it.

21:20 Offspring that can't make small RNAs still resist viruses
The experimental design is clean enough to read by color: use a fluorescent virus, and if the virus replicates successfully the nematode turns green, and if it is destroyed it stays black. First let nematodes get infected and destroy the virus, then knock out the machinery for making small RNAs in their offspring — these offspring cannot make small RNAs from scratch themselves. Then infect them with the same virus. If they still stay black, the only explanation is that they inherited small RNAs from their parents. That is exactly what happens: all the offspring stay black, and the resistance carries on for several more generations. Sequencing can read those small RNAs directly, matching the viral genome, and only the offspring of parents that had been infected have them. These nematodes have no T cells or B cells; they defend against viruses with RNA, and this mechanism is RNA interference, which won the Nobel Prize in 2006.

24:46 The brain and heredity don't speak the same language
The boldest question in this episode is: can the brain leave information for the next generation? Rechavi points out the obstacle is translation — the brain stores information in the three-dimensional structure of synaptic connections, while any heritable information must squeeze through the bottleneck of a single cell, the fertilized egg. He also offers another possibility: learning something might just mean removing a particular odorant receptor, in which case one RNA controlling that receptor would be enough to pass it on; such phenomena have been reported in mammals, but he says they haven't been convincingly enough demonstrated, because no one has explained how information gets from the brain to the germ cells. His own route bypasses translation: in a 2019 Cell paper, changing only the production of native small RNAs in the nematode brain altered the foraging behavior of offspring, affecting them down to three generations later, with the mechanism landing on the sage-2 gene in the germline, and also requiring the protein that physically carries RNA.

28:17 Mammals lack an RNA amplifier
Why can nematodes do it while mammals must be doubted? The mechanism Rechavi gives is blunt: the nematode's secret is that it can keep amplifying these small RNAs, so the signal doesn't get diluted. In mammals there is no known comparable amplification mechanism, so the question becomes — how does a tiny bit of RNA affect the whole organism? One possibility is that it acts only very early in development: when there are just a few cells, perhaps even acting on the placenta formed during pregnancy, and from there gradually steers development off course, with problems like metabolism following. This is the ‘developmental origins of health and disease’ line of thinking. He also frames RNA's role in mammals as a candidate rather than a conclusion: small RNAs are the leading candidate for transmitting protective or harmful effects of stress, but ‘in mammals we don't know, time will tell’.

31:07 RNA is more plastic than DNA, so start with diagnostics
Applications come in three layers. The nearest is diagnostics: in Israel, most couples preparing to have children get DNA diagnostics for genetic diseases, but right now no one looks at RNA; if the mechanism were clearer, RNA would be another layer, a whole new world, and there might be certain RNAs associated with disease. The advantage is that it isn't fixed the way DNA is — DNA is yours, and if you can't change it you can only choose another embryo; RNA is plastic. Only a step further out is intervention: in rodent experiments, overfeeding causes problems in the next generation, but if you make the mice exercise, this abnormal inheritance is corrected; when doing IVF, perhaps you could change the RNA composition of the things you introduce. Rechavi is restrained about the timeline: he says this doesn't happen now, it's science fiction, but if it were figured out, he has also imagined telling someone preparing for IVF, ‘you should go run on the treadmill for a while’, and that would change your RNA profile.

item.title: Stolen Goods Sell for 70-80% of Retail, and Retail Theft Is Now an Industry
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-oddlots-偷来的货能卖到原价七八折-零售盗窃已经产业化/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-oddlots-偷来的货能卖到原价七八折-零售盗窃已经产业化/
item.description: Stolen merchandise passes through two layers of hands: boosters are recruited to steal from stores, and fences clean off the markings and resell the goods, which then show up on secondhand platforms. Connected goods fetch 70-80% of retail; T-shirts and deodorant only 30-something percent.
item.content:encoded:
Stolen merchandise passes through two layers of hands: boosters are recruited to steal from stores, and fences clean off the markings and resell the goods, which then show up on secondhand platforms. Connected goods fetch 70-80% of retail; T-shirts and deodorant only 30-something percent.

High information density: Home Depot's head of asset protection breaks down how shrink is categorized, the real P&L of locking up shelves, the pricing patterns of stolen goods, and the progress of federal legislation — with plenty of hard numbers.

8:19 A third of shrink is self-inflicted
Home Depot splits shrink into two buckets: operational/administrative and malicious — in Scott's phrasing, the things we do to ourselves versus the things others do to us. At Home Depot, about 30% of shrink falls into the former, with the rest on the malicious side. The industry line that has circulated for years: of malicious shrink, about 40% is caused by internal employees, 35% by people who walk into the store, and the remainder is self-inflicted operational shrink. These percentages only move within a few points each year, but he thinks they are drifting upward, and that it has been underreported ever since COVID — neither police reports nor the FBI's Uniform Crime Report fully capture it.

22:52 Employees are explicitly told not to chase anyone
The bigger problem isn't money, it's people. Scott says professional criminals often use homeless people and addicts to go into stores and steal; these people have one thing on their minds — getting the goods out to exchange for money — so they will fight, and they have fought. People have been injured in Home Depot stores, and even killed. That's why asset protection staff are trained in de-escalation, and the 400,000 store employees are explicitly told not to intervene — just back off. His attitude: he'd trade shrink for human safety every single day, and management and the board would back that decision.

23:53 RFID dies the moment it enters a steel store
Joe asks why RFID has been talked about for 25 years and yet in 2026 is still expensive and hard to scale. Scott says he doesn't understand it either, but explains Home Depot's particular problem: it's a hardware store, and the store is full of steel, essentially a Faraday cage, so passive RFID can't be read — you have to use an active-signal approach. He also says tag cost is now almost zero; the real bottleneck is the reading hardware — covering a 140,000-square-foot sales floor with eight separate entrances and exits is extremely costly. They've tried the idea of bricking merchandise before it leaves the store, but retrofitting an entire production line for a single drill is very hard to scale.

25:58 Stolen goods have been pushed onto secondhand platforms
The division of labor works like this: boosters are recruited and given a list, cash, or the promise of drugs, then go steal from stores; the goods go to a fence — maybe a garage, a warehouse, or a flea market — who strips the price tags, store markings and electronic tags before reselling, and the money flows up to whoever runs the operation, which might be a small crew of a few people or a transnational gang. After the INFORM Act took effect in 2023, big platforms like Amazon and eBay were required to verify seller identities, so stolen goods shifted to Craigslist and Facebook Marketplace, because the law left a gap that doesn't cover peer-to-peer sellers. Home Depot works backward from the platforms, using models to flag sellers pricing below cost while moving large volumes.

35:19 One combo kit sold means restocking 4.2 times
Whether to lock up shelves is a financial question. Scott says they look at the data: there's a combo kit priced at $799, and for every one sold, they have to restock 4.2 times. Take that to finance and they immediately get it's a gross margin problem — as long as it breaks even or even makes a little, locking it up is justified. But half of Home Depot's revenue comes from professional contractors, and if they break a bit on the job site, rush to the store and find it out of stock, that's a loss too. So they lock up a carefully selected set of categories, with a QR code to summon an associate, who opens the lock in an average of 90 seconds; and locking things up doesn't necessarily hurt sales — in some categories sales actually go up, because the goods are finally in stock.

39:23 A fake bill of lading can drive the goods right out
In the supply chain he counts three plays: first, pure diversion, where whole containers are rerouted at the port or transload warehouse and taken elsewhere, sometimes even loaded back onto a container ship and shipped away; second, a driver drives eight hours across state lines, and while he sleeps someone pries open the trailer doors and moves boxes; third, forged bills of lading and pickup orders, made to look real with AI, where a driver pulls in, says he's picking up a certain trailer, and just drives off. He says what's new isn't necessarily the methods, it's the volume, because these cases are very hard to pursue. Rail is the area that has clearly worsened over the past five or six years — cars sitting in a yard get pried open by a group; and the other side has good intelligence, they don't touch every car, only the one carrying guns or electronics.

41:28 AI in security is an efficiency tool
Scott says they have more cases than they can investigate, so for them AI is an efficiency question: a typical organized retail crime case takes an average of 70 days from discovery to closing and handing over to police, and compressing that cycle means they can work more cases. They just replaced the video management system across all 2,300 stores, letting existing cameras run edge analytics — identifying people who linger too long in an area, deliberately avoid associates, or show up where they shouldn't be. He also admits that to identify a particular combination of suspicious behaviors and then recognize the specific person, he doesn't have enough cameras yet, but they will get there. Separately, they have an in-house company doing web scraping.

44:30 Seven years ago no one cared; now there's a federal bill
He says he's very optimistic now. INFORM is arguably the first federal bill driven by organized retail crime, and next is CORCA (Combating Organized Retail Crime Act): the retail industry broadly supports it, it's bipartisan, it has passed the House, it's attached to the NDAA awaiting Senate passage, and the president has said he'll sign it. The rationale is that this crime is inherently interstate — it happens in Cobb County, Georgia, and the goods flow to South Carolina and North Carolina, which is interstate transportation of stolen goods, but there were no corresponding federal resources; the bill would provide resources, prosecutors and a coordination center. Seven years ago he was thoroughly pessimistic about this: no one took it seriously, and the prevailing mood was decriminalization and defunding the police.

item.title: Baseball's stadium music isn't accompaniment — it's how fans take the game back
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-throughline-棒球场的音乐不是伴奏-是球迷抢回比赛的方式/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-throughline-棒球场的音乐不是伴奏-是球迷抢回比赛的方式/
item.description: Baseball's official historian thinks stadium music is too loud, but it was fans singing Hey Hey Goodbye in unison that rattled the opposing pitcher — music turns spectators into part of the game.
item.content:encoded:
Baseball's official historian thinks stadium music is too loud, but it was fans singing Hey Hey Goodbye in unison that rattled the opposing pitcher — music turns spectators into part of the game.

Medium information density: the first half is baseball music history, and only the back half — the Nancy Faust story — is worth the price. Worth listening for anyone into sports, live experience, or fan culture.

0:00 One walk-up song can turn a passerby into a fan
Host Randa Abdel Fattah says she was indifferent to baseball for most of her life, until Mets pitcher Edwin Diaz's walk-up song Narco in 2022 changed that. Diaz is a closer, usually entering at a key moment in the late innings, and the team uses his walk-up song to announce to the opponent: the show's over, this one's ours. The entrance video went viral, the team started handing out plastic trumpets to fans, the mascots Mr. and Mrs. Met pretended to play trumpets, and eventually the team flew the original artist, Timmy Trumpet, in from Australia to perform live. The host says that if you were in the stands at that moment, the feeling was electric.

6:18 The official historian thinks the ballpark is too loud
MLB's official historian John Thorne says plainly that he doesn't like entrance music. What he misses is the quiet between half-innings — quiet that lets other sounds ring louder and clearer: the strange sound of a bat hitting a baseball, the same sound when Babe Ruth hit, and when Josh Gibson hit; the dull thud of a leather glove catching a fly ball; a coach yelling at a player to keep running and steal second. He thinks nonstop audio, the endless contest for fans' attention, may have robbed a kid who goes to the ballpark to dream of that right.

10:31 Take Me Out was originally a women's suffrage song
The seventh inning stretch was originally literal: stand up, move your legs, get the blood flowing. It became a musical moment thanks to a 1908 song, Take Me Out to the Ball Game, which was actually about women's suffrage. The protagonist of the original lyrics is Katie Casey, a baseball fan who knows all the players' names, gets upset when the umpire makes a bad call, and when the score is tight knows exactly what to do — she gets the whole crowd to sing along. From this came a whole new genre, the "baseball song," which flooded sheet music, cylinder records and 78s in the 1910s.

12:35 The 1910s baseball song boom was publishers, not fans
John Thorne points out that the wave of baseball music in the 1910s was less about fans liking it than about publishers liking it — it was essentially a marketing tool to pull people into the ballpark. The evidence is the number of copycats: George M. Cohan released Take Your Girl to the Ball Game almost the same week, followed by imitations like I Want to Go to the Ball Game. But despite all the baseball songs Tin Pan Alley produced, large-scale singing in actual ballparks remained rare, and John says the main reason was technical: sound systems were too primitive, and before radio took hold, a brass band was still the best accompaniment.

17:47 That 1977 singalong broke the opposing pitcher
On a muggy July night in Chicago in 1977, the White Sox were down two runs to the Kansas City Royals. After the White Sox put runners on first and second, someone in the stands started singing Hey Hey Goodbye, it grew louder, more than 45,000 fans joined in, and the announcers had to raise their voices to be heard over the singing. The White Sox then erupted — bases loaded, bases cleared, four runs in — and the other side was forced to change pitchers. As the pitcher walked off the mound, Chicago fans "saw him off" even louder. Nancy Faust says she was thinking, "Did I hear that right?" because this wasn't the kind of thing you normally heard at a ballpark — it was more like mockery.

23:51 She gave players their songs; fans fed her ideas
In her first years with the White Sox, Nancy Faust still played a set repertoire: the national anthem, Take Me Out to the Ball Game, and the hour when the crowd filed in. In her third year she started improvising, playing whatever she saw. When Dick Allen came up, the crowd would leave the bathrooms and the popcorn stands, so she played the then-popular Jesus Christ Superstar, and when he hit a home run the place went crazy. Fans sitting around her booth started feeding her ideas: one player had worked at a watch counter, the store closed and he got stuck there, so when he came up she played Does Anybody Really Know What Time It Is. She says she was "the soundtrack to whatever was happening," not just scoring the players.

25:52 An opposing pitcher admitted the singing shook his confidence
After that 1977 singalong, one opposing pitcher told reporters: you're standing on the mound, there are men on base, Zisk is in the batter's box, thirty thousand people are singing Kiss It Goodbye — that shakes your confidence. Nancy Faust later read in a book that players recalling those years said they hated hearing that sound, and flinched when they heard na-na-goodbye. And White Sox slugger Richie Zisk said of those same fans: I don't know if they came to see us or we came to see them, but I can tell you it fired us up. Nancy's conclusion: I guess I did have an impact, I just didn't know it at the time.

28:56 She can't read music — it's all by ear
Every song Nancy Faust improvised over her career, she did by ear — she can't read music. Hum a few bars of anything and within seconds she'd play it back on the organ. She retired from the White Sox organist job in 2010, White Sox fan and former President Barack Obama personally wrote to congratulate her on her career, and the booth she occupied for decades is now named after her. She still occasionally comes back for special occasions, like Pope Night, playing Gotta Have Faith and Don't Stop Believing.

item.title: Iron Age Ireland had no Celtic invasion, only trade and language
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-ancients-爱尔兰铁器时代没有凯尔特人入侵-只有贸易和语言/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-ancients-爱尔兰铁器时代没有凯尔特人入侵-只有贸易和语言/
item.description: The traditional story says Celts brought iron to Ireland around 500 BC, but archaeology finds almost no trace of incoming migrants — Celtic identity was really a language community that grew slowly out of a Late Bronze Age maritime trade network.
item.content:encoded:
The traditional story says Celts brought iron to Ireland around 500 BC, but archaeology finds almost no trace of incoming migrants — Celtic identity was really a language community that grew slowly out of a Late Bronze Age maritime trade network.

Medium information density, with a long setup in the first half. The real value is in the second half, on Celtic identity, sacral kingship and the Fianna warband, suited to listeners interested in pre-Roman Europe.

2:18 Why the Irish Iron Age is the murkiest period
John Waddell says the Irish Iron Age is the darkest stretch of Irish prehistory, partly because people at the time cremated their dead. In much of Europe people were buried with large quantities of fine grave goods, and cremation plus burial destroys a great deal of useful archaeological evidence. So despite very fine metalwork and monuments, the absence of burial evidence makes this history especially hard to read. He also points out that using the term "Celtic Iron Age" for this period amounts to sticking an ethnic label on an era, adding another layer of trouble to an already complicated story.

9:28 Sea routes connected people rather than isolating them
Waddell repeatedly stresses an underrated fact: in prehistory, waterways were channels connecting people, not barriers. Ireland and Britain are both islands, and people habitually assume islands mean isolation, but coastal routes and river routes were very likely the main means of connection. Before the Romans built straight roads, travel by water was far easier than travel by land. This means we have consistently underestimated how connected the populations of prehistoric Britain and Ireland were. The Irish Sea itself was a connecting force, and the English Channel linked England to the continent.

10:31 Sacred sites sat on high ground, not by rivers
Tristan asks whether Iron Age settlements were all near rivers and coasts. Waddell's answer is unexpected: famous sites like Tara, Rathcroghan and Navan Fort are not obviously on major routes. Each sits on high ground in its own different way, and these locations may have carried a kind of sanctity since the Neolithic. Tara was already an important burial place before 3000 BC, and its story runs into the medieval period, representing more than 4000 years of ritual activity. The importance of these places came from accumulated time and religious meaning, not from rivers and sea routes.

15:38 A sacral king who fails or is wounded is deposed
Waddell draws a key concept out of medieval Irish texts: sacral kingship. The king of Tara was not a political strongman; his fundamental duty was to maintain cosmic order. If a sacral king could not bring good harvests, he was deposed. Another feature was that his body had to be flawless: once a sacral king was wounded, scarred or deformed, he was deposed. Waddell thinks this ritual may eventually be traceable in the archaeology of Britain and Ireland, suggesting that in the Celtic era, the pre-Roman period, certain tribal rulers did carry a sacred quality.

21:43 The Celts were not invaders but a language community
The traditional story is that around 500 BC a Celtic-speaking people brought knowledge of iron to Ireland. Waddell says this is wrong. His best definition of the ancient Celts is "people who spoke Celtic," not an ethnic or racial definition. Ireland in the pre-Roman period was undoubtedly Celtic-speaking, but archaeology finds almost no evidence of incoming migrants in the Iron Age or the Late Bronze Age. Instead, from around 1000 BC there is abundant archaeological evidence of trade and exchange between Britain and Ireland, with the Thames, the Rhine, the Rhône, the Saône, the Ruhr and the Danube all serving as major corridors. Trade and exchange means movement of people, and people carried myths, legends and language with them. The Celtic languages most likely took shape gradually amid this Late Bronze Age surge of connectivity.

31:04 The Banquet Hall is actually a ceremonial processional way
On the hill of Tara there is a monument called the "Banquet Hall," a pair of very long parallel earthworks. Waddell's colleague Conor Newman established that it was never a banquet hall — it is far too large to be any kind of hall. Standing between the banks, you find you cannot see the world outside, because the banks are still high even in their ruined state. Newman proposed that it was a processional way running from the northern end of the hill to the centre of the summit, used for royal inauguration rituals. There are gaps in the banks that let the procession look left and right at the burials and other monuments on either side, reminding the man about to become sacral king of the stories of his ancestors and predecessors. Waddell compares it to Rome's Appian Way, lined on both sides with tombs.

33:07 Beneath Tara lies a timber circle larger than Stonehenge
Geophysical survey on the hill of Tara revealed a huge circular timber structure, four to five times the scale of Stonehenge. It was built around 2000 BC and at the time would have stood on the hilltop as prominently as Stonehenge, but today there is no trace of it on the ground — only aerial photographs show the faint outline of the circle. Waddell says this reminds us that large timber circles earlier than Stonehenge are a feature of the prehistoric landscape of Britain and Ireland. Tara's burials have another detail: many of them intersect one another, as if new graves were deliberately laid partly over old ones to connect with ancestral remains, both legitimising one's own existence and conveying some kind of story.

39:22 The forgotten king Dathi and a Swiss myth
Waddell tells the story of an almost forgotten king, Dathi, associated with Rathcroghan in western Ireland. In medieval legend Dathi was the last pagan king of Ireland, said to have campaigned on the European continent, possibly reaching the foot of the Swiss Alps, and to have been struck dead by lightning at the foot of the Alps, with his body carried back to Ireland and buried at Rathcroghan. The story was especially popular in the 19th century, because some people took it as proof that Irish military power reached far overseas. But Waddell says it looks like pure fabrication: there never was an Irish invasion of Switzerland. Dathi most likely only raided Britain occasionally. He was later overshadowed by the more famous warrior Cú Chulainn and gradually forgotten.

item.title: Ashurbanipal's Library: He Was Both a Tyrant and the Earliest Book Collector
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-stuffmissed-亚述巴尼拔的图书馆-他既是暴君-也是最早的藏书家/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-stuffmissed-亚述巴尼拔的图书馆-他既是暴君-也是最早的藏书家/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: Ashurbanipal locked defeated kings in dog kennels and forced people to make bricks from their ancestors' bones — and he also built humanity's earliest systematic library, keeping the Epic of Gilgamesh alive to this day.
item.content:encoded:
Ashurbanipal locked defeated kings in dog kennels and forced people to make bricks from their ancestors' bones — and he also built humanity's earliest systematic library, keeping the Epic of Gilgamesh alive to this day.

Medium information density; the first half is Mesopotamian background, and the second half — how the library was preserved and deciphered — is where the real value is.

0:01 The same man, two completely opposite first impressions
At the British Museum, Tracy read the exhibit panels on Ashurbanipal's library and thought, "this guy's library is astonishing"; in the same gallery Patrick read the other set of panels about him as king of Assyria, and came away thinking, "this guy was really cruel." The same body of material can support two entirely opposite impressions at once, and the rest of the episode pulls that contradiction apart: he really did yoke the defeated king of Elam to his chariot and shut a rival up in a dog kennel, and he really did order texts from across the empire copied and sent to the capital.

4:04 You cannot lay out a Mesopotamian timeline at all
Tracy wanted to open the episode with a basic timeline and found she couldn't. Mesopotamia spans more than three thousand years from the first cities, with civilizations, kingdoms and empires overlapping and influencing one another, so a linear timeline is itself a distortion. Assyrian history is divided into Early Assyrian (from about 2600 BCE), Old Assyrian (from about 2025 BCE), Middle Assyrian (from about 1363 BCE) and Neo-Assyrian (911 to 609 BCE), followed by a post-empire period. Assyrian people still exist today: roughly three to five million people in Iran, Iraq, Syria and Turkey identify as Assyrian.

9:10 The father split the empire in two to prevent civil war
Esarhaddon's father Sennacherib had razed Babylon completely and even diverted canals to flood the ruins, and was later assassinated by his own sons — read as divine punishment for destroying Babylon. Esarhaddon rebuilt Babylon and positioned himself as its "governor" rather than its king. In 672 BCE he divided his two sons' roles: Shamashumukin took Babylon, Ashurbanipal was made crown prince of Assyria. The arrangement was meant to prevent a repeat of the civil war that had attended his own accession. The episode says explicitly that this will come back later — because the brothers eventually turned on each other.

9:10 He got an education a king was not supposed to get
Ashurbanipal's education had already begun when he was made crown prince. He learned horsemanship, chariot driving, archery, military tactics and court etiquette — the standard royal package. But he also learned literature and history, knew multiple Sumerian and Akkadian dialects, and could read and write cuneiform. The episode stresses that kings of this era were not usually educated this academically, and often were not literate at all — literacy was the business of scholars and scribes. The likely reason he got this education is that early in life he was not being groomed entirely as the heir.

13:14 In the reliefs, he wears writing tools on his belt
Ashurbanipal was a patron of the arts, building temples and palaces and commissioning vast numbers of reliefs. Many depict him in battle, lion hunting, and daily life amid wealth and luxury; some show the severed heads of enemies. The episode singles out one detail: in many depictions he wears a riding stylus tucked into his belt, including in scenes where he is killing lions with a sword — Holly jokes that he probably wanted to write in his diary after killing a lion. The reliefs from his reign are considered the peak of Assyrian art, and the lion-hunt reliefs are now in the British Museum.

15:19 Cruelty was not his invention — he took it to the extreme
The episode draws a clear distinction: practices like displaying enemies' severed heads were normal among rulers of ancient Mesopotamia; but in his own commissioned depictions and in the records others left, Ashurbanipal is seen as having pushed this to an extreme. Specific examples include: salting the land after putting down a revolt, forcing people to grind up their ancestors' bones to make bricks for a palace, making the defeated king of Elam pull his chariot in the triumph, and forcing one rival to live in a dog kennel. About that rival, some accounts say he was forced to wear a dog collar, others that a chain was run through his jaw.

21:39 This was the earliest "systematic collection" library
The library was built in the capital, Nineveh, and tablets have been found in the Southwest Palace, the North Palace, and around the temples of Ishtar and Nabu. The episode stresses two things: first, it is unclear whether these were the library's original storage locations or the result of tablets scattering after the city's destruction; second, this is one of the earliest known libraries to be systematically acquired and organized — a deliberately collected, curated repository of knowledge, and the largest collection of Assyrian texts in the world. Excavations yielded more than twenty thousand tablets and fragments, many bearing standardized colophons, indicating a systematic method of labeling and cataloguing. The total number of complete tablets is in fact unknown.

22:39 He ordered the whole empire to hand over books — and knew who to ask
Ashurbanipal ordered temples and palaces across the empire to send texts to Nineveh, usually by having a copy made, with him receiving the copy or the original. Surviving documents show he actually wanted the originals, and that subordinates may have "creatively misinterpreted" the instructions in order to keep originals in their own temples or collections. Surviving correspondence also shows he knew exactly where to look for texts he wanted, and who might hold works he did not know about but that were worth acquiring. Holly describes him as having a network of scholarly acquisition librarians. Some texts in the library were written by him, and many tablets carry colophons in his hand.

item.title: There are no irreplaceable leaders, only irreplaceable luck
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-tyler-没有不可替代的领袖-只有不可替代的运气/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-tyler-没有不可替代的领袖-只有不可替代的运气/
item.description: Diamond says history has no irreplaceable leaders — Genghis Khan just happened to be born when the steppe was at its wettest in two thousand years. But people like Rachel Carson and Resnick really did move things forward by ten or twenty years.
item.content:encoded:
Diamond says history has no irreplaceable leaders — Genghis Khan just happened to be born when the steppe was at its wettest in two thousand years. But people like Rachel Carson and Resnick really did move things forward by ten or twenty years.

Diamond is 89, talking about leaders, geographic determinism, Papua New Guinea and Bach cantatas. Medium information density, but the passages on environmental optimism and writing method in the back half are the most valuable.

1:09 There are no irreplaceable leaders, only irreplaceable timing
Diamond's answer to ‘who is the most irreplaceable leader in human history’ is ‘no one.’ The reason is not that leaders don't matter, but that time washes out the differences: Jesus was a charismatic founder, but the Roman Empire of the same period had half a dozen other prophets; Genghis Khan built the largest land empire from China to Poland, but recent research found that the wettest period on the steppe in the past two thousand years fell right around his birth — had he been born twenty years earlier or two hundred miles farther away, we would never have known his name. From this Diamond draws a distinction between two kinds of questions: why you and I speak English right now has its answer in the domesticable plants and animals of the Fertile Crescent, nothing to do with individuals; why Amazon is what it is today has its answer in Bezos alone.

13:50 Rachel Carson moved the environmental movement forward by ten years
Cowen challenges Diamond with the environmental Kuznets curve: once per capita income hits 28,000, countries naturally turn green — is Carson replaceable? Diamond concedes the movement would have come anyway, but stresses that she at least moved it forward by about ten years — the day after Silent Spring was published, a senator announced a government investigation into toxic chemicals. More crucial was her position at the time: in that era a professional scientist writing popular science was seen as ‘selling out,’ and she was not a university professor, so no one could say that of her; she was a woman, wrote like a poet, and would read her drafts aloud to hear them. Diamond says that even today's best science writer, Richard Dawkins, does not write as well as she did.

18:00 The pomegranate juice industry waited five thousand years to appear
Cowen tests Diamond's replaceability theory with the pomegranate juice industry: without the Resnick family, America would eventually have gone down this road anyway. Diamond says no. Pomegranates were domesticated five or six thousand years ago, but there was never a global pomegranate juice industry, because pomegranate juice is extremely hard to make — you cut an orange and squeeze, but the pomegranate's value is inside an extremely hard rind, and the contents are not pulp but small seeds; scale production requires a three-story-tall tower that crushes whole pomegranates rind and all. In 2002 America had 22 pomegranate growers, 21 of them small farmers with no money and no incentive. Lynda Resnick put in about two hundred million dollars and waited 18 years before starting to make money. Companies like Coca-Cola and Nestlé would never allow a division to invest 150 million dollars and lose money for 18 years.

29:32 Face-to-face social skills are in cliff-edge decline
Diamond's advice to a 25-year-old who wants to become influential: learn to talk to people face to face, put down indirect communication tools. He has done 60 years of fieldwork in Papua New Guinea and watched Chevron bring in international lawyers from Switzerland to negotiate with villagers who had never left their village — the lawyers thought they'd close the deal in a day, but the agreement reached on day one was met on day two with the villagers saying ‘we've forgotten that agreement, the people who signed it don't count, these are a few other negotiators.’ The villagers had negotiated face to face their whole lives and had far more skill than the international lawyers. Diamond says that over the past 40 to 50 years he has watched social skills degrade, and in his 39-year-old child's generation it is especially striking, because most communication is no longer face to face and people no longer understand each other.

33:54 New Guineans may be smarter than Westerners
Diamond answers ‘yes’ outright, and says some people hate him for it. His argument is that natural selection pushed in different directions: over the past ten thousand years European survival depended mainly on surviving smallpox, tuberculosis, measles and other infectious diseases, which has little to do with being smart; the main causes of death in New Guinea were coping with an extremely difficult environment and coping with other New Guineans — warfare there was constant. So his impression is that New Guineans on average ask more questions and are smarter. He adds that Westerners usually think they are stupid because they use stone tools — but they lack metal tools because agricultural output was much lower, not because of intelligence. Cowen presses him on a Nature paper claiming West Eurasians have gotten smarter since the Stone Age; Diamond says he hasn't seen it, but for more than a century eugenicists have been trying to prove Europeans are smarter, with no evidence whatsoever.

39:24 The Industrial Revolution happened in Britain because it is an island
Diamond rejects Greg Clark's hypothesis that the British became more patient by intermarrying and lowering their time preference. His explanation is geography: Britain is an island, needs no standing army, and is not constantly invaded — the last successful invasion was 1066. Not needing an army, it gradually developed democracy, and democracy is a productive form of government. Britain also sits on the Atlantic coast, and like the Netherlands, Spain and Portugal, it was one of the countries able to spread across the world, because the Atlantic coast was the testing ground for seafaring technology. He notes that in the 1600s Britain cut off its king's head and Parliament became powerful. On Daron Acemoglu and Jim Robinson's extractive vs inclusive institutions theory, Diamond says he has learned more from Jim Robinson than from any individual in the past 20 years, but thinks they give geography less weight than he does.

44:32 Big business and young people have made him cautiously optimistic
Diamond says that 20 years ago he would have said the most evil and destructive force in the world was big business, which at the time basically didn't care about the environment. But over the past 20 years big business has come to care more and more: Walmart leads on sustainable products, Unilever leads on sustainable fisheries, even oil companies. In 1999 the World Wildlife Fund sent him to do an environmental study of Chevron's oil field in Papua New Guinea; he expected it to be terrible, but found Chevron extremely cautious, because they knew that if they screwed up, New Guineans would sue them and they wouldn't get the Norwegian oil field development contract. Another source of optimism is young people: 25 years ago young people didn't care about the environment, now they care very much. He gives the odds as 51% good outcome, 49% bad.

47:46 The most important question is not to find the most important question
Cowen asks what the biggest environmental problem is at the global macro level, and Diamond laughs and says this is what makes interviewing Diamond frustrating: his answer is always ‘the most important thing is not to go looking for that one most important thing, because the world is complicated.’ He uses marriage as an analogy: a couple about to marry asks what the single most important thing for a happy marriage is, and the answer is not to go looking for that one most important thing — you need to get 37 things right, and if you get 36 right but are incompatible on sex or religion, the marriage breaks. Back to the question itself, he says there are three things we must get right: climate change, inequality, and nuclear risk — including the risk of nuclear war and nuclear winter.

item.title: AI Is a Rounding Error for Ordinary People: Diffusion Takes Fifty Years, Backlash Won't Wait
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-interconnects-ai-对普通人是舍入误差-扩散要五十年-反弹却等不了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-interconnects-ai-对普通人是舍入误差-扩散要五十年-反弹却等不了/
item.description: The Industrial Revolution gave ordinary people cheap clothes and sewing machines; AI so far gives them fun images and better search — the benefits are too indirect, and the political backlash is arriving too fast.
item.content:encoded:
The Industrial Revolution gave ordinary people cheap clothes and sewing machines; AI so far gives them fun images and better search — the benefits are too indirect, and the political backlash is arriving too fast.

An eight-minute short take, not especially dense, but it offers a counterintuitive angle: the biggest risk to AI isn't technical failure, it's that ordinary people can't feel the benefits.

0:00 AI is still a rounding error in daily life
The author spent a few weeks on his honeymoon without touching AI at all, and on returning realised: the points where ordinary people encounter AI are either marginal or confusing. The positive impressions are making fun images and an enhanced Google search; the negative ones are addictive social media algorithms, a friend of a friend hooked on an AI chatbot, and various claims about data centers. Family, food, transport, entertainment — the core of daily life — have barely changed directly. His conclusion: being obsessed with AI is the result of a very small number of people actively choosing it, and stepping outside the bubble reveals that what's happening today really doesn't matter that much to most people.

0:00 The Industrial Revolution gave physical things; AI gives indirect benefits
The first Industrial Revolution brought cheaper clothes, cookware, reading material and new livelihoods; the second brought sewing machines, food preservation, indoor plumbing, photography, better light sources, bicycles and electrification — a long list, and a very physical one. The author worries that even if AI's benefits materialise (new scientific discoveries, treatments for rare diseases, sustained economic abundance), they are too indirect: ordinary people won't credit OpenAI or Anthropic with saving their life, because it was their family doctor who told them about the new treatment; and not many Americans will care that OpenAI solved the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem. He judges that fifty years from now, the daily life of the average American will still look a lot like today.

3:47 AI today is mainly a tool serving elites
Knowledge work is roughly half the US economy, and for that half AI is already (or soon will be) as foundational as electricity; rapid agent improvements over the next eighteen months will accelerate this. But a transformative, highly productive tool that only lifts half of society is highly unstable. The author cites the "Engels' pause": from 1790 to 1840 British workers' wages stagnated while GDP per capita grew rapidly amid technological upheaval. He argues that if the AI industry itself thinks this is the closest analogy, then backlash from those who don't benefit is legitimate. He also agrees with Doug O'Laughlin's judgment: knowledge-work output explodes while headcount in the tech industry very likely shrinks.

3:47 The backlash isn't rooted in AI, it's Big Tech's old debts
The author splits the political backlash facing AI into two layers: first, the early positive effects are too indirect; second, they are deeply intertwined with Western society's historical grievances against Big Tech. He stresses that the latter merely collided with AI in time — if AI's exponential growth had happened decades after the growing pains of platforms like Google and Meta, the data center issue very likely would never have risen to such a central political position. Solving either one would greatly relieve the pressure and give the industry more time to show positive reasons. And AI itself, through doom rhetoric and declarations of mass unemployment, has marked itself as a negative or unsafe technology, making both harder.

3:47 Robots might rescue the narrative for LLMs
The author raises an ironic possibility: if the intelligence explosion from mass-producing large language models spills over into robotics and accelerates the spread of robots in daily life, humans will quickly seize on AI's tangible benefits. This is ironic because many people have been working hard to convince the public that this LLM wave is very different from the general AI progress of the past ten or twenty years. If in the end the same dynamic saves (or largely overshadows) the LLM narrative, that would be funny. He also cautions that the connection between robotics, autonomous driving and the current AI revolution is currently more a matter of storytelling.

3:47 Diffusion takes fifty years; the fight against it won't wait
The author calls the present the first five years of a fifty-year diffusion process, and lays out two simple problems: the positive effects are too indirect, and the political backlash is entangled with Big Tech's history. He judges that the story of diffusion will last far longer than the struggle against it. Young people paying attention today will, within their lifetimes, see powerful AI go from effectively 0% to over 90% full adoption. What truly marks AI's evolution is the kind deeply integrated into enterprises and acting as a personal assistant; it is only just becoming viable, and adoption will be far slower than for easily understood applications like ChatGPT. So continuing to push the technology forward is crucial — the benefits are astonishing but not guaranteed, and there is still a great deal of hard work to do on distributing them widely.

item.title: Grok Bot shipped in a month: a small team hid in a cave, a big team would have micro-decisioned it to death
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-lennys-grok-bot-一个月做出来-小团队躲进山洞-大团队会拖没微决策/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-lennys-grok-bot-一个月做出来-小团队躲进山洞-大团队会拖没微决策/
item.description: Building knowledge work into Cursor is not obviously wrong, but users can smell three visions sharing one screen — that is shipping your org chart. So Grok Bot started from zero, a handful of people hid in a cave for a month.
item.content:encoded:
Building knowledge work into Cursor is not obviously wrong, but users can smell three visions sharing one screen — that is shipping your org chart. So Grok Bot started from zero, a handful of people hid in a cave for a month.

The first half is the trade-off detail of product decisions; the second half — that a bot should have its own computer, that automation should have no UI — is worth more.

0:02 Shipping a hit in a month came from a small team hiding in a cave
Grok Bot did not start as a tab added to Cursor. It started as a team of "a handful of people" isolated in a corner of the office with a private Slack channel, going from first line of code to an internally usable prototype in about a month. Roman's judgment: with a big team and a 6-to-12-month vision plan, you would not have built the thing that actually shipped — because every day is a pile of non-obvious micro-decisions, and a big team drags those decisions to death.

9:07 Not putting it in Cursor, because users can smell three visions on one screen
Building knowledge work into Cursor is not obviously wrong, and the team discussed it seriously. Roman says the problem with that path is "small paper cuts": the product feels oppressive to non-technical users, plus the brand association. He called out the competitor approach of "add a tab for every new form factor" — users can feel that this is not one unified vision of work but three visions sharing one screen, like "shipping your org chart." So they decided to start completely from zero.

11:08 Two or three hundred manual onboardings, so the same mistake never happens tomorrow
The team onboarded two or three hundred people by hand, including the host. The first few were painful: the computer wouldn't start, the user was confused, and the core team had to sit on that 20-minute call. Roman says the effect of that presence is "that can never happen again" — it has to be fixed tomorrow, because tomorrow you onboard the next person. This mode lasted about two weeks.

12:08 They deliberately did not tell users what bots to build
Internally, a pattern emerged on its own: "5 to 10 bots each owning a piece." By the end of the second week, people started promoting a standout bot to primary personal assistant, then making it chief of staff and dispatching tasks to the other bots — there was even a screenshot of a user telling a bot it had been promoted, and the bot asking whether that came with a raise and a bigger token budget. The team noticed, but deliberately did not guide it in onboarding, afraid of biasing users; they wanted to see whether outside users would get there on their own, and many did.

14:09 Not showing the thinking process is a product stance, not laziness
Grok Bot hides a lot of internal machinery: no tool calls, no step-by-step view of what it clicks on its own computer, just a Slack-like activity indicator and on-demand stage updates. Roman's analogy: you would not ask a colleague to report second by second which button he pressed and which website he visited. Some feedback did ask for a to-do list and priorities, but nobody wanted long streams of text and chain of thought, which confirmed the direction.

19:11 Those three weeks of internal beta were mostly unshipping
From internal beta to public launch was only about three weeks, and Roman says that stretch was "we unshipped a lot": cutting experimental features, moving pseudo-developer visibility tools off the product surface, like interfaces that exposed the model's internal thinking and specific memories. The test was "what is the launch post" — if it can't be written as a compelling launch tweet, it probably shouldn't be built. He also distinguishes "Grok Bot now has" (new button, new dropdown, new integration) from "Grok Bot can now" (new capability); the latter is the right frame.

29:17 Automation should have no UI; 99% is generated from one sentence
Competitors' automation setup means going into a sidebar, clicking plus, picking a trigger event, picking an action. Roman calls that clunky, and the result is that people rarely actually build automations. Grok Bot's approach is to define it in natural language: tell the bot "remind me every morning at 8," and it should just do it — the user should never see the automation-creation UI. Today 99% of automations on the platform are built that way.

30:17 Two early decisions: everything in the cloud, every bot has its own computer
Roman credits Grok Bot's success to two decisions that were not obvious at the time. First, users should never have to think about local versus cloud, whether their computer is on, or whether starting from their phone means connecting to the machine at home — all of it goes to the cloud, and the bot becomes a persistent colleague with its own computer, consistent across every entry point. Second, the bot must have its own computer, because a huge number of tools have no decent MCP or API, and humans never worked through MCP and APIs anyway — they clicked pixels and typed into input boxes.

item.title: Picky Eating Isn't the Food's Fault: Fix the Relationship, Then Talk Nutrition
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-secureattach-孩子挑食别怪食物-先修关系-再谈营养/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-secureattach-孩子挑食别怪食物-先修关系-再谈营养/
item.description: The feeding strategy itself matters less than how you execute it; a parent's own relationship with food is the most effective intervention for their child.
item.content:encoded:
The feeding strategy itself matters less than how you execute it; a parent's own relationship with food is the most effective intervention for their child.

Medium information density, but the "health impact tiers" framework and the practical advice on "neutralizing food" offer direct relief to anxious parents.

5:05 The feeding anxiety starts at the nine-month checkup
Jennifer is a registered dietitian who did nontraditional work in the USDA's SNAP education program and considered herself someone who "knew how to feed a child." At the nine-month checkup the doctor said her child's weight wasn't keeping up, and she said it felt like the rug was pulled out from under her. For years afterward she worked to keep her kids on the growth curve, and her second son showed early signs of extreme picky eating. Standing in the kitchen making lunch, she realized she couldn't be the only parent struggling this much, and in 2019 she started Kids Eat in Color, initially posting feeding tips as a hobby.

12:12 The research behind "don't pressure your kid" isn't that strong
She says "don't force your child to eat" is a great slogan, and for some families that one line is enough. But after digging deep into the research on feeding pressure, she believes it isn't as strong as dietitians or feeding experts make it out to be, and parents actually have more room to experiment. The second part of her book specifically addresses "what if the standard approach doesn't work": first give the general advice, then give the alternatives that are considered less ideal but can be executed with reduced risk, which she calls risk reduction.

16:19 Put a small piece of green pepper on the plate five hundred times
The exposure method she teaches parents: put a small slice of green pepper on a plate full of foods the child likes. The goal isn't to get him to eat it, but to desensitize him to the pepper's presence. Maybe after five hundred times he'll sniff it, then lick it, then throw it at his brother, then one day eat it. The precondition is that the child is in a regulated state — if the child isn't soothed, he simply can't try new things, because he's scared of something else. So first get the child calm before he sits down at the table.

23:22 An anxious child has a dry mouth and tight throat and physically can't eat
Sarah adds the neural mechanism: when anxious, the mouth goes dry, the throat tightens, and there may be nausea or stomach pain — these are exactly the signs of sympathetic (fight or flight) activation, while eating requires the parasympathetic rest and digest state. In other words, if every time you come to the table it's with dread and a power struggle, you're physiologically pushing the child in the opposite direction of eating. Play, jokes, and little table games work because they bring the child into that relaxed, connected parasympathetic state, and only then do saliva and swallowing come back.

28:26 A meal can be rescued from the worst possible start
She tells of one dinner at her own home: before the parents even got back to the table, the two kids were already fighting, and one slammed the door and went to his room. They let that child calm down on his own in his room while the remaining three ate first. Fifteen or twenty minutes later the child came downstairs and started eating, the whole family was laughing, and everyone was eating. She says the meal ended with the siblings fighting again, but the moment of connection in the middle was real. So don't hold yourself to perfectionism — there's usually at least one good moment in a meal, so find it.

32:28 Sensational headlines can basically be swiped away
The first filter she gives parents: if the headline is sensational, you can almost certainly conclude it's wrong, probably about ninety percent of it is taken out of context, so just keep scrolling and don't lose sleep over it. But if it's a real event — say an outbreak of diarrhea one summer, or a specific food recall — then pay attention. What she really wants to give is a tiered framework: the first tier is severe food allergies and insufficient calorie intake (ARFID, extreme picky eating, food insecurity), which can make a child very sick or worse and must be addressed first.

33:29 Protein and fiber are in the second and third tiers, food dyes in the fourth
The second tier is protein, and every meal and most snacks should have a real protein food. The third tier is fiber, because fiber trickles down: if a child eats enough high-fiber foods, he'll naturally eat less of the added sugar and added sodium. And food dyes, which grab the most headlines, are in the fourth tier, with a very narrow impact. She says that for the vast majority of children, artificial dyes won't change their health trajectory; for the small number of sensitive children, parents have probably already figured it out themselves. Removing dyes from the food system wouldn't solve the childhood health crisis either.

43:35 Call it a "cookie," not an "occasional food"
To help parents who don't have a healthy relationship with food, her entry point is "talking about food with facts": call foods by their names directly — this is a cookie, this is a sandwich, this is your chicken, this is your sugar. Don't say "this is an occasional food, this is an everyday food," don't sort your child's food into healthy/unhealthy or good/bad, and avoid moralizing and black-and-white thinking. She says there's no evidence that black-and-white thinking directly causes eating disorders, but research has found that black-and-white thinking is very common in children with restrictive eating disorders, and hearing "foods are good or bad" gets embedded in their restrictive thinking.

item.title: Making Your Rivals Depend on Your System Is How America Has Won for Three Centuries
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-ilt-让对手依赖你的体系-是美国赢了三百年的秘密/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-ilt-让对手依赖你的体系-是美国赢了三百年的秘密/
item.description: The Dutch, the British and the Americans took turns as hegemon not by blockading rivals but by getting them to stake their survival on someone else's maritime order — once they can't live without the sea lanes and the markets, cutting them off becomes the most effective weapon short of war.
item.content:encoded:
The Dutch, the British and the Americans took turns as hegemon not by blockading rivals but by getting them to stake their survival on someone else's maritime order — once they can't live without the sea lanes and the markets, cutting them off becomes the most effective weapon short of war.

Walter Mead breaks America's three-century winning streak into a five-step strategy and pushes it all the way to China, the Taiwan Strait and AI deterrence. What you get is a durable judgment framework, not news-cycle opinion.

4:47 Unpredictability is a form of power
‘Unpredictability’ is not madness; it is a modern strategy of power. Mead says post-Cold War American diplomacy held itself up as a pillar of stability by ‘letting the whole world know where America's red lines are’, while Trump profits by doing the opposite: crossing lines, threatening allies, turning commitments into bargaining chips. He saw through a secret of the information age — the marginal cost of lying: the first lie is expensive, the thousandth is nearly free. When Clinton was engulfed by the Lewinsky scandal, he discovered that shame only lives in other people's minds; as long as you keep walking, the dogs bark but the caravan moves on. Trump took that insight to industrial scale. The cost is borne by the American diplomatic system: when the world's number one power turns itself into the unpredictable card, every alliance and rule built on predictability after World War II is coming apart faster.

10:00 The last step of global hegemony is cutting the cord
The Anglo-American maritime order did not win through some battle; it won through a five-step playbook. First, an open society on an island — the 17th-century Dutch tolerated heretics and Jews, and ideas and capital poured in. Then global trade: Dutch merchant ships sailed the world, and the wealth was so great that even the paintings are full of Turkish carpets and Brazilian parrots. Third, while continental powers fought over inland Silesia, you seized India and Canada across the globe. The fourth step is the riskiest: instead of copying Spain and sealing off your colonies, you invite the whole world in to do business, the British navy suppresses pirates, and every merchant ship benefits; Germany and Japan were likewise invited in after the war. Only the last step is the hole card: once the other side cannot live without your grain, your rubber and your shipping lanes, you cut it off — Germany discovered in World War I that Argentine grain and Malayan rubber had all been cut off, and its economy promptly collapsed.

16:38 Everything China does is to avoid having the cord cut
Look at China through the same framework and you find Beijing is well aware of its own jugular. Mead says: suppose the mainland blockades Taiwan, and the US counter-blockades from a hundred miles off Taiwan's coast — oil cannot get in, manufactured goods cannot get out, soybean contracts with Brazil and Argentina are voided, and China's economy is strangled alive. He has discussed these things with officials and scholars at Chinese universities, and this worry is always present. So China's energy policy has to be read in parallel: on one hand building oil reserves so large they surprise outsiders; on the other throwing up solar and hydropower while digging as much coal as possible. It is not schizophrenia, it is one thing: pulling out, one by one, the soft spots of ‘dependence on the outside world’. He also warns the US not to retreat into isolationism — agriculture and AI both need overseas markets to keep themselves alive.

25:50 Every round of technology needs a new institution to match
Mead starts from the ownership society: at America's founding there were independent farmers with land everywhere, and while a bridge is nice it means my taxes go up — that trade-off is itself a political education. The railroad era was matched by the Homestead Act, with the government giving land to railroad companies and farmers, and a national market grew out of it; in the 20th century what replaced the family farm was the single-family suburban house, paired with tax-exempt municipal bonds and highways, becoming a new wealth-distribution machine. Now that machine has run into housing prices: young people cannot afford to live near where they work. His remedy is remote work and autonomous driving. When the commuting radius expands from 40 miles to 75 miles, usable land for housing rises with the square of the radius, and the physical space opened by technology is enough to carry two more generations. But the precondition is filling in the ‘infrastructure’ of institutions — he coined the word info-structure, meaning the institutions and regulatory rules that let AI actually land in hospitals and courts.

40:22 Silicon Valley is defecting to the Tech Hamiltonian camp
American foreign policy debate has for centuries been four vocabularies: Hamiltonians want a strong state clearing the way for capital, Wilsonians want to spread liberal democracy, Jeffersonians fear a bigger government, Jacksonians stay isolationist in peacetime and fight to the death when hit. The post-Cold War establishment was a marriage of Hamilton and Wilson, but Trump brought Jefferson and Jackson into the game. Mead says the new species truly worth noting is the Tech Hamiltonian. In the 1990s tech companies loved to say ‘we are a global company, Google has no borders, Washington has no say’; AI competition has turned tech into a contest of national destiny. Economic positions changed too: the old multinational car companies wanted borderless labor and markets, while Silicon Valley wants supply-chain and IP security, and even wants its employees to be patriotic, to feel that selling code to China is shameful, and that colleagues will report you outright. The core of business has shifted from the old multinationals to tech nationalists, and this is the underwater current of America's political realignment.

50:00 The power with the most equipment fears technological turnover most
Mead has been to Ukraine twice. The first time he visited a drone factory and saw them converting children's toy trucks into ground drones carrying mines to blow up tanks; a few months later he went again, and the progress was unimaginably fast. The battlefield is now a gray kill zone, usually only two or three soldiers move together, and one of the hardest problems is ‘how to get the wounded out’ — you need to build a ground drone with a metal shield to drag people, with a squad of drones alongside hunting the enemy drones coming to attack. He heard of one wounded soldier who took 63 days to be evacuated from the front. Things flip every six months. The bitter irony for the US: the power with the most tanks and aircraft carriers is precisely the one that fears this kind of parameter revolution most — legacy equipment turns from an advantage into a relocation cost. Russia's Black Sea Fleet has no great battle to fight, yet it is bottled up at home by Ukrainian small boats and drones.

54:16 The new variable worth watching most in the Taiwan Strait is Japan
On ‘will the mainland attack Taiwan’, Mead's judgment is that Beijing needs a very high probability of success before it is willing to cross the threshold — failure would be catastrophic for the initiator. But between ‘attack’ and ‘do nothing’ there is a long gray ladder: for example requiring all merchant ships bound for Taiwan to first stop at mainland ports for customs clearance, or imposing a soft blockade, doing things that change facts enough without triggering an armed US response. The real new variable on the Taiwan board is not America's attitude but Japan. The Japanese have already publicly concluded that if China takes Taiwan, Japanese independence is finished too; they are raising defense budgets, rewriting security doctrine, reshaping the national psyche. Historically Japan turns very fast when faced with a real threat. How steep Japan's learning curve is, and whether Beijing must factor Japan into its calculations, is the key to the Taiwan question in the coming years.

1:10:00 AI actually makes deterrence more credible
Moving Cold War deterrence logic into the algorithmic age, Mead points to a counterintuitive corollary: deterrence succeeds or fails on making the opponent one hundred percent believe that ‘if I do X, you will necessarily do Y, and you can do it and are willing to’. As long as there is a human veto point in the decision chain — ‘I might go soft when the time comes’ — that commitment has a crack. Automating part of foreign-policy decision-making and handing it to AI turns retaliation into an executable mechanism that will not hesitate — and deterrence becomes more credible. But this is the doomsday machine problem from science fiction: decisions of civilizational scale no longer require a human to bear the consequences. His own assessment of the question is ‘very interesting and a little confusing’, and he does not think the answer has appeared yet.

item.title: ECT Is Not What You Think: A Century of Drift from Back Room to Routine Treatment
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-tpwky-ect-不是你想的那样-从密室到常规治疗的百年漂移/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-tpwky-ect-不是你想的那样-从密室到常规治疗的百年漂移/
item.description: Modern ECT is a procedure performed under anesthesia and muscle relaxants, with strong efficacy, but the evidence on memory-loss side effects is still not fully clear, and social misunderstanding has left it over-stigmatized.
item.content:encoded:
Modern ECT is a procedure performed under anesthesia and muscle relaxants, with strong efficacy, but the evidence on memory-loss side effects is still not fully clear, and social misunderstanding has left it over-stigmatized.

If your image of ECT is still stuck on One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, this episode will completely reset it. Hear the actual procedure, the indications, the side effects, and one expert's clinical account.

8:07 What actually happens if you or I get ECT
If you or I were to receive ECT, here is how it goes: first a risk assessment and informed consent, then a physical exam, then an overnight fast. The next morning, in a hospital or outpatient setting, you get an IV line and two blood pressure cuffs (one on the arm, one on the right leg), and you're hooked up to EKG, EEG and EMG. After the anesthesiologist puts you to sleep, the leg cuff is inflated to restrict blood flow to the right foot, then a muscle relaxant such as succinylcholine is given. Once the muscles are fully relaxed, a bite block is placed, and then a brief pulse of current is delivered through the electrodes (lasting seconds, or even half a second). The goal is not to make your whole body convulse, but to induce a generalized seizure, typically lasting 25-70 seconds. Because the muscles are already relaxed, you see almost no external movement — the whole thing is obvious on the EEG.

14:15 Where the electrodes go, and why the right side first
There are several electrode placements: bitemporal (like in the movies), bifrontal, and most commonly 'right unilateral' — one electrode on the right temple, the other on the right side of the top of the head. Right unilateral is used for most people because it produces fewer cognitive side effects. Why consider the right side first? Because for about 98% of right-handed people and 70%-90% of left-handed people, language function sits in the left temporal lobe. Avoiding electrical stimulation on the left side theoretically reduces language-related memory problems. But right unilateral is slightly less effective than bilateral. During a course of treatment, doctors switch based on side effects and efficacy: if bilateral side effects are heavy, switch to right unilateral; if right unilateral isn't working well enough, switch to bilateral.

16:20 Seizure threshold and the effective dose
The seizure threshold is the minimum amount of current that will induce a seizure. There is no precise measuring device, so you start by estimating from age, then titrate up from a low dose until a seizure appears. But treatment isn't just about reaching threshold — the effective dose is usually 2.5 to 5 times the threshold. With bilateral, 2.5 times is enough, while right unilateral needs 5 times, because unilateral stimulation has a harder time achieving the same effect. The dose varies from person to person and has to be adjusted as you go. If in one session a patient's seizure doesn't occur or doesn't last long enough (under 25 seconds), the doctor may increase the dose and try again. Treatment is generally three times a week, with a full course of 6 to 18 sessions, sometimes longer.

20:22 We still don't know exactly how ECT works
Why does shocking the brain treat depression and catatonia? Frankly: we still don't fully understand. There are several main hypotheses. One is neurotransmitter change: after ECT, serotonin, dopamine and GABA (an inhibitory transmitter) all change markedly. The rise in GABA is itself anticonvulsant, which could explain why the seizure threshold rises and seizures get shorter over a course of treatment. Two, large fluctuations in hormones such as ACTH, prolactin and TSH are seen in the hypothalamus and pituitary. Three, ECT promotes neurogenesis, with BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) as a key molecule. But how these changes directly relieve symptoms still has no one-to-one mechanism. The mechanisms may also differ across conditions (depression, schizophrenia, catatonia), so for now the only option is to keep researching.

24:24 Depression data: far better than first-line antidepressants
For treating severe depression, ECT's key numbers are quite strong: most studies report remission rates (symptoms fully gone) of 50%-60%, and response rates (marked improvement) of 60%-90%. By comparison, the best remission rate for SSRI antidepressants is only about 40%. ECT has another uncommon benefit — it can cut the 30-day readmission rate by half. This is not to say it should be first choice, nor that it has no risks (relapse or symptom rebound within 6-12 months is still not rare); but in patients with treatment-resistant depression combined with severe suicide risk, these efficacy advantages are hard to ignore.

26:27 Among side effects, memory problems draw the most concern
ECT's thorniest side effects center on cognition and memory. Right after the procedure there is brief confusion lasting from a few tens of seconds to half an hour, and for weeks there may be declines in attention and executive function. Interestingly, most cognitive function actually improves in the long term — possibly because the depression improves. The real trouble is memory. Anterograde amnesia (difficulty forming new memories) mostly recovers within a few weeks after the course ends, which is why many people are restricted from driving or making major decisions during treatment. Retrograde amnesia (losing past memories) is what worries patients more: it usually affects recall of the most recent months or even years before treatment, and in most cases recovers, but in some it is permanent. Bilateral treatment is more likely to cause this than right unilateral.

34:55 Catatonia: a frequently misread, potentially fatal syndrome
Catatonia is often lumped in as a subtype of schizophrenia, but it is actually a psychomotor syndrome that any psychiatric or neurological illness can trigger. Patients appear awake, eyes open, yet are almost completely immobile and mute; they may show posturing or waxy flexibility (an arm placed in a position stays there). Because they cannot eat or drink and remain immobile for long periods, they are prone to malnutrition, pressure sores, muscle contractures, and even death. Untreated catatonia has a mortality rate as high as 20%! The most common treatment is benzodiazepines, but ECT is extremely effective in catatonia from many causes. The girl with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis mentioned earlier (the 'Brain on Fire' case) developed catatonia; immunotherapy and lorazepam both failed, and she ultimately recovered with ECT.

48:36 The biggest bottleneck isn't efficacy, it's access
Dr. Lopez believes the biggest obstacle ECT faces today is finding a place to get it. His hospital performs more than 6,000 treatments a year across two campuses, averaging about 10-12 sessions per patient. But it is not widely available across the US, and adults and children traveling across state lines for care are not few — especially in infants, children and adolescents with catatonia from autoimmune encephalitis, where finding an experienced treatment team is extremely hard. So improving access is his greatest hope. At the same time, doctors on other internal medicine, pediatric and critical care teams often don't recognize catatonia and don't dare, or don't think, to call an ECT consult; so 'preaching' to non-psychiatric colleagues is part of his daily work.
