item.description: Fan Shiguang, who shot two seasons of Qian Lang, says most marriages end up lukewarm or worse, and growing old together to the very end is rare. What we lack most isn't stories — it's money, and the habit of seeing old people as specific human beings.
item.content:encoded:
Fan Shiguang, who shot two seasons of Qian Lang, says most marriages end up lukewarm or worse, and growing old together to the very end is rare. What we lack most isn't stories — it's money, and the habit of seeing old people as specific human beings.

The first half is the two hosts talking, more feeling than information; the second half is the director interview, dense with killed story ideas and behind-the-scenes detail. Start at 41 minutes.

4:08 Five million in inheritance, and the law fights the deathbed wish
An elderly woman with no close family died in a Shanghai nursing home. She had done an advance guardianship notarization with notary Li Chengyang, but left no will. Sorting her belongings, the notary found she had left five million, including a apartment, cash and passbooks. She had said repeatedly that she wanted to donate it to society and not give it to relatives, but that wish had no legal form. Li Chengyang chose to follow the law and look for statutory heirs, tracing through archives to children and relatives she hadn't seen in years. The notary office was split internally too; some colleagues thought her wishes should simply be respected. The compromise was to propose to the inheriting children that 200,000 of the five million go to a fund helping old people with no one to rely on. The children agreed.

11:55 Whether they slept together decides whether the inheritance can be given
An elderly man with a terminal illness gave advance guardianship and his estate to a woman who had cared for him for years and was not a relative. He had a biological daughter. The notary office argued fiercely over it, and one key point was whether the two slept together: if they didn't, the caregiver was just a nanny or a live-in housekeeper, and an old man leaving his estate to his nanny was morally acceptable; if there was a sexual relationship, it stopped conforming to public morals. The caregiver was herself married, but had had no contact for years, so in effect the marriage didn't exist. So it became an open-relationship question, and the notary office didn't want to take on the risk of indecency for making that judgment.

16:02 Old people finding partners increasingly don't register the marriage
Li Kangmei, the subject of episode two, was with Lao Li for eighteen years without ever registering the marriage, and there was no de facto marital relationship. The hosts found this far more common than they had imagined: after divorce or the loss of a first marriage, many older people entering a new relationship choose not to marry. They don't necessarily say they love the person; they say they want companionship, someone to take care of them, and behind that is a fairly deep loneliness. Lao Li already had a terminal illness, and Li Kangmei's choice was whether to stay to the last moment or leave early because there was no de facto marital relationship.

24:46 Reality TV forces you to pick a side every five minutes
The hosts contrast documentary with reality TV: much of the tension in reality TV is manufactured, backed by a very strong narrative — knowing the audience's view of mama's boys, for instance, so a mama's boy is kneaded into the show. This destroys the audience's tolerance for the complexity of real intimate relationships: every plot beat, every five minutes, demands a position, and that position must be the morally correct one, then projected onto some character, and wherever that character goes you're on his side. Documentary works the other way: it shows that no one has it easy, some characters get more screen time and some less, but you can see everyone's difficulty, and quite a few of them appear pixelated and anonymous.

34:20 The older generation says I sleep badly, not I'm depressed
Medical anthropologist Arthur Kleinman found that young people today have a rich psychological vocabulary and can quickly say I'm depressed, I'm anxious, I'm a bit bipolar; but older people, even when expressing psychological needs, still use somatized language — I've been sleeping badly, I have a bit of a headache — and won't say I sleep badly because I think too much, that I'm a little depressed. The hosts explain: in our culture it's easier to talk about physical pain, everyone gets a headache or a cold, there's no stigma; once you talk about depression and anxiety, it's a different order of stigma and pain.

43:53 The idea that got killed: she just wanted to play mahjong
Director Fan Shiguang tells a story he killed himself: the most diligent auntie in a hospice ward, whose husband had bladder cancer and not long to live. She took the bus in at seven or eight every morning and left at five or six in the evening, like going to work, but you couldn't see love on her face — she just asked doctors and nurses again and again how much longer other people's family members had. Only later did they learn her son had died of a heart attack two years earlier; she was a shidu family, and her tears had probably run dry two years before. Someone asked what she wanted to do after her husband died, and she said she wanted to play mahjong, because he had never let her. The first scene shot after the husband died was her finding workers to smash the legs off a two-meter bed with a sledgehammer, one by one, and buying a mahjong table to put in that spot. The story was never used, because the team couldn't find her real inner world — they only had part of the facts.

52:28 Growing old together is rare, not the norm
Fan Shiguang says the team did fieldwork sitting with roughly fifty families, across two seasons, and found that going from youth all the way to growing old together to the very end is not the norm — it's rare. Most marriages are lukewarm, or worse. He tells the story of the first season's episode Lovers: an old man with Alzheimer's loses control and hits his wife; the daughter forcibly sends him to a specialized nursing home; the old woman sneaks off to visit every few days, and the hospital won't let her come because it upsets him. After the old man is sent to hospital, gravely ill, the old woman finally gets her chance to wait on him — cutting his nails, washing his hair, washing his feet. A month or so after he dies, she says through tears: I looked down on him my whole life. When I was young I was a good student and he was a poor one; my family were intellectuals and his were workers; he insisted on courting me, and I had no way out, and in the end I muddled through a whole life with him.

1:04:18 Learning to drive at 95, and one sentence takes the right away
Fan Shiguang says the team worked hard to break stereotypes, because people love to divide into groups and stick on labels — old people are like this, they're just confused — and there is deep prejudice in that. In season one there was a 95-year-old man learning to drive and taking the license test. Fan thought about it and realized he had unconsciously said, "driving is fine, but he is 95 after all," then asked himself: in that sentence of mine, 95-year-olds are stripped of their rights — as if he doesn't deserve it. Public Security Ministry regulations don't say a 95-year-old can't learn to drive, but in that verbal violence the right is taken away. The episode's bullet comments were full of: can this old man really be allowed on the road, he's so selfish, what if he hits someone — and all that worry rests on prejudice.

item.title: The Supreme Court Gave Students Constitutional Rights, Then Handed Searches and Paddlings Back to the Schools
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-stuffmissed-美国最高法院先给了学生宪法权利-后来又把搜包和体罚还给校园/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-stuffmissed-美国最高法院先给了学生宪法权利-后来又把搜包和体罚还给校园/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: From refusing to salute the flag to opening a purse, six cases gradually drew the constitutional rights of American public school students; the Supreme Court laid down that schools are not totalitarian enclaves while also upholding corporal punishment and reasonable-suspicion searches, narrowing the boundary of those rights.
item.content:encoded:
From refusing to salute the flag to opening a purse, six cases gradually drew the constitutional rights of American public school students; the Supreme Court laid down that schools are not totalitarian enclaves while also upholding corporal punishment and reasonable-suspicion searches, narrowing the boundary of those rights.

Each case gets five or six minutes laying out the background and the holding, suited to listeners who want to grasp in one sitting where American public schools draw the lines on speech, corporal punishment and searches.

5:10 The flag-salute case: student rights enter the school for the first time
Can students really invoke the First Amendment during class? This case actually begins with religion: Jehovah's Witnesses families held that saluting the flag violated the commandments against having other gods and against graven images, and refused to pledge or salute the flag. In 1940 the Supreme Court had ruled against them, and World War II pushed more school districts to require students to salute and recite the pledge of allegiance daily. West Virginia expelled students who refused the pledge, labeled them delinquents, and their parents could be fined or even jailed. In 1943 the Supreme Court overturned the earlier ruling 6 to 3, and Justice Jackson wrote the opinion on Flag Day: orthodoxy in politics, nationalism, religion or other matters of opinion is not to be defined by any official; students need not utter words they do not believe, nor make empty gestures. This was the first time the Court established that students hold some First Amendment rights inside school.

11:21 An official prayer is ruled unconstitutional
In the Cold War the United States cast itself as a God-fearing nation, added Under God to the pledge of allegiance in 1954, and more public schools began reading scripture or praying before class. In 1951 the New York State Board of Regents asked religious leaders to co-write a short, non-denominational prayer, with each district deciding whether to adopt it. Districts that used the prayer let students opt out, but the parents of 10 students still sued. In 1962 Engel v. Vitale held it unconstitutional 6 to 1; the key was not whether it was compulsory but that the prayer was written by the government, which itself constituted establishing religion. Justice Black quoted Madison: it is proper to take alarm at the first experiment on our liberties; the same authority that could establish Christianity to the exclusion of other religions could just as easily establish one Christian sect. The ruling triggered fierce backlash, and the plaintiff families were mocked and harassed.

18:31 An armband is constitutional expression
In December 1965, middle and high school students in Des Moines planned to wear black armbands to class to protest American involvement in the Vietnam War. School officials announced in advance that refusing to remove them would mean suspension, and some students — including four siblings — wore the armbands anyway and were suspended. In 1969 the Supreme Court ruled for the students 7 to 2. The issue was that this was not ordinary dress or grooming but quiet, passive expression close to pure speech, and it did not disrupt class. Absent evidence of actual or provably imminent substantial interference with instruction, school officials may not suppress student opinion. The ruling said: public schools may not be totalitarian enclaves, and students and teachers do not shed their constitutional rights at the schoolhouse gate. This substantial disruption standard later became the baseline for free speech on campus. Justice Black dissented that students would from then on resist almost every school rule, and the host said on the show that this slippery-slope argument sounds rather absurd.

24:40 A school-funded newspaper can be cut
In 1983 two pieces in the Hazelwood East High School student newspaper The Spectrum troubled principal Reynolds: a story on teen pregnancy that used pseudonyms but might still allow the interviewees to be identified, and a divorce story that named and criticized a student's parent. Reynolds decided to cut both full pages rather than just remove the articles, on the grounds that there was no time to revise and the paper had to come out before the semester ended. In 1988 the Supreme Court ruled for the school 5 to 3. The key distinction was between tolerating student speech and promoting it: this newspaper was funded and published by the school, readers would take its contents as endorsed by the school, and the two pieces were indeed ethically immature as journalism. The Court held that schools may exercise control over what they promote. The rights established in Tinker thus acquired their first clear boundary.

29:46 Corporal punishment is not an Eighth Amendment matter
Host Tracy suddenly recalled that many of her childhood teachers kept wooden paddles on their desks, and on looking it up found that corporal punishment has still not disappeared in the United States. In the 1977 case Ingram v. Wright, the school's paddle was under two feet long, three or four inches wide and half an inch thick, with one to five swats in principle; but Ingram was struck more than 20 times in a single incident and needed medical attention. The Supreme Court did not dwell on whether that instance was excessive, ruling instead that school corporal punishment does not violate the Constitution. The reasoning was that the Eighth Amendment protects the convicted, and the harsh facts of criminal conviction and imprisonment separate prisoners from schoolchildren; schools are open places, with teachers and classmates as witnesses, and students go home at the end of the day. According to NEA figures, corporal punishment remains legal in public schools in 17 states and is actually practiced in 14, with boys, Black students and students with disabilities struck at significantly higher rates.

33:52 Searching a bag needs only reasonable suspicion
In 1980 in New Jersey, a 14-year-old student known as TLO was reported by a teacher for smoking in the restroom. Vice principal Choplik searched her purse, saw cigarettes and rolling papers, kept digging, and found what appeared to be marijuana and evidence of drug dealing; TLO was ultimately convicted and given a year's probation. In 1985 the Supreme Court upheld the search 6 to 3. The ruling acknowledged that the Fourth Amendment binds school officials and that students have a privacy expectation, but that it must be balanced against the school's need to maintain a learning environment. So school searches need not meet the probable cause required of police, only the lower threshold of reasonable suspicion. The teacher's report that TLO was smoking gave the vice principal reason to suspect she had cigarettes, and a purse is exactly where they would be; seeing rolling papers naturally extended the suspicion to marijuana, which was equally reasonable.

item.title: To Make Criticism Land, Lead With High Standards and Trust
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-thinkfast-批评想被听进去-先给高期待与信任/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-thinkfast-批评想被听进去-先给高期待与信任/
item.description: Getting criticism believed isn't about opening with a few compliments — it's about letting the other person see that the standard is high and that you believe they can reach it. In one experiment, a single line — "the standard is high, but I know you can meet it" — pushed Black students' rate of actually revising their essays to the top.
item.content:encoded:
Getting criticism believed isn't about opening with a few compliments — it's about letting the other person see that the standard is high and that you believe they can reach it. In one experiment, a single line — "the standard is high, but I know you can meet it" — pushed Black students' rate of actually revising their essays to the top.

The originator of stereotype threat research breaks down the mechanism himself and grounds the intervention in a replicable experimental script. Twenty minutes of high information density, with none of the vague communication chicken soup.

1:04 Identity bias makes people underperform on the spot
When a situation carries a negative label about one of your identities, and the thing at stake matters to you, you worry you'll be judged by that label. That worry comes from the situation itself: it depresses performance on tests, sports or intellectual tasks in the moment, and it makes people avoid such situations over the long run, which in turn shapes who they befriend, where they live, and where they send their kids to school. The anxiety doesn't come from ability; it comes from the expectation of being defined by the label.

3:10 Social media lets labels chase you from every direction
Social media's power lies in how fast it spreads thumbnail sketches of group images, and people have no patience to see the full picture and the exceptions. So it naturally multiplies the number of situations where you feel you'll be seen through your identity. Occasionally it also spreads images that reduce threat, but the overall tone skews negative — the result being that in a diverse society, everyone is more on guard about their own identity and about what others might be thinking.

6:16 A 15-minute self-affirmation exercise lifts grades
In racially integrated classrooms, Black students live with the constant possibility that their ability is being underestimated. Teachers asked seventh graders to spend just 15 minutes writing a short essay about the people and things they valued most. White students were barely affected, but Black students used the occasion to let the teacher know "I'm not just that label," and their grades began to rise — setting off a positive feedback loop: grades improve → vigilance about the label drops → grades improve further. The intervention cost almost nothing, yet it changed long-term trajectories.

9:20 Vigilance in diverse settings: remember or forget
The author calls this state churn. In settings where people of different backgrounds are together and the outcome matters, people get pulled back and forth between two choices: remember that "others might read me through my group's stereotype" to protect themselves, or simply forget it, relax, and trust the person in front of them. This isn't fragility; it's the real pressure the situation imposes. When the setting matters, it continuously drains attention that should be going to the task.

12:24 High standards plus trust make feedback work
In the experiment, students wrote an essay about their favorite teacher and received critical feedback. Under the first two approaches — giving it straight, or prefacing it with a "positive cushion" — white students trusted it, while Black students were highly distrustful. The third approach simply added one line: "We have high standards, because these essays are going to be published; I read your essay and I believe you can reach them." Under that condition, Black students took their essays home to revise at three times the rate of the other conditions.

14:26 You can't assume others already trust you
After years as a dean and provost, Claude considers the most useful skill to be realizing that everyone you work with needs that signal of respect. Society's common mistake is assuming trust already exists, when in reality people worry about how you view the group they belong to. Truly effective leaders are all good at giving that signal first: even if an employee disagrees with a decision, as long as they feel the other person respects who they are and their potential, the team atmosphere is completely different.

17:35 Let people see you're human before you talk trust
Claude breaks good communication into three things: first, let the other person know you understand what this situation means to them — when power is unequal, the person with more power has to send the safety signal first; second, near-obsessive clarity, because beating around the bush destroys valuable information; third, warmth and goodwill, because people need to confirm there's a good person across from them before they'll hand over trust. Matt sums it up as connection, clarity, care.

item.title: Latin Doesn't Make Surgeons: Exams Should Be Hard at Something Useful
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-econtalk-拉丁文练不出外科医生-考试难-不如考得有用/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-econtalk-拉丁文练不出外科医生-考试难-不如考得有用/
item.description: Latin doesn't make surgeons: skills barely transfer. If you assume harder material sharpens the mind, a nation's brightest get wasted on the most useless knowledge — that is the lesson of the Qing examination system.
item.content:encoded:
Latin doesn't make surgeons: skills barely transfer. If you assume harder material sharpens the mind, a nation's brightest get wasted on the most useless knowledge — that is the lesson of the Qing examination system.

It puts imperial civil-service exams, military selection and modern transfer experiments on a single chain of evidence, unusually connecting history with talent assessment — and the two sides genuinely clash.

10:03 Wrong exam content dooms a nation even with brilliant candidates
Hong Xiuquan failed the Qing examinations at least four times. After the last failure, he had visions on the road home, believed himself the brother of Christ, and eventually launched the Taiping Rebellion — which Daisy says may be the deadliest civil war in human history, with deaths around thirty million. He was not alone: examination seats were far fewer than the number of candidates, many sat into their forties and fifties without passing, and the only way home was to teach. Daisy adds that the deeper cost fell on those who did pass: they mastered the eight-legged essay while knowing nothing of the science and mathematics transforming the world. When the brightest young men can only drill a dead format, the country bleeds from both directions.

22:51 British civil-service reform was elites replicating themselves
The Northcote-Trevelyan report is often seen by the British as the founding document of the modern civil service, but Daisy backs the revisionist judgment: in the name of a unified exam, it pushed Oxford and Cambridge classics graduates into key posts. Benjamin Jowett, master of Balliol, worked behind the scenes to place his classics students throughout the empire. Michael Coolican's "No Tradesmen and No Women" points out that the 1854 report reduced the most naked buying and selling of offices, but also snuffed out the professional exams that departments had been growing. Exams aren't the problem; what they test decides whether they select the able or select people like yourself.

35:58 A bureaucracy without price signals corrects itself through corpses
Daisy attributes bureaucratic failure to the absence of feedback: no price mechanism, no profit and loss, so a department cannot tell whether its program saves or kills. The military sounds like a counterexample, but military bureaucracies err just as steadily in peacetime; almost every time Britain went to war after a long peace, the first year bred a crisis — the shell crisis of early World War I being one. What actually forces correction is not internal inspection but mass death on the battlefield. She calls it a crueler error-correction mechanism than prices. To make a bureaucracy reliable, you first need a signal that shows consequences; otherwise no amount of rigor in selection can save the quality of everyday decisions.

43:06 The Royal Navy won by testing navigation, not Latin
Daisy notes that Britain's real pillar in the Victorian era was not the army but the Royal Navy. As early as 1677, after a run of defeats by the Dutch, Samuel Pepys set an oral exam for captains: three senior officers questioned a candidate face to face on how to command a ship. Over the following century, navigation, charting and trigonometry entered the written exams, and chart-makers like Nelson, Cook, Flinders and Bligh passed through that gate. Daisy draws out two exam traditions: Pepys tested skills needed immediately; Macaulay and Northcote-Trevelyan later tested classical languages. One served safety at sea, the other served a layer of status — naturally the effects differ.

47:31 Content doesn't matter? Macaulay's screening argument misses the key link
Here comes the highlight: Daisy reads Macaulay's 1833 parliamentary speech aloud. The gist: whatever a age happens to teach, the best at it will necessarily be the cleverest, most industrious and most honor-seeking of the young; so Cambridge could teach Ptolemy instead of Newton and its top students would still be excellent; teach Cherokee instead of Greek and the best Cherokee scholars would still be the finest; even astrology and alchemy would do. Another MP praised it on the spot as the most practically wise speech in parliamentary history, but Daisy says flatly: this is eloquence running away with him, and it completely misses that what you learn really does matter.

51:21 Dead twigs and corn: wrong content makes discipline just watering
Daisy closes on Macaulay with the 1917 rebuttal of the American medical educator Abraham Flexner. Flexner said the devotees of mental training are like Egyptian priests: they stick a row of dead twigs in the soil and then water them on schedule for the sake of discipline. Plant corn and the discipline is no less, with a crop thrown in. Against the American medical schools of the day, where many aspiring doctors were forced through Greek and Latin before touching a medical book, Flexner's answer was: medicine is already hard enough, and using it to sharpen the mind is far more efficient than using dead languages. Daisy agrees: spend the best years of the most gifted on what has been disproved or is useless, and the winners will be the rivals who let their young learn real knowledge.

59:21 Rectangles don't train triangles: transfer needs identical elements
Thorndike designed a cleaner controlled experiment: have people repeatedly estimate the area of rectangles until they clearly improve, then have them estimate the area of triangles — almost no transfer. Even between two shapes that close, it fails, so the claim that classical languages sharpen the mind is even less credible. Thorndike's explanation was identical elements: transfer appears only when old and new tasks share the same components; far transfer essentially breaks down. Daisy draws the exam-design principle: to select people who can navigate, test navigation and trigonometry; to select people who can practice medicine, test medicine. An exam that actually works wires difficulty directly into the real task.

item.title: Global liquidity peaks: the companies that spent most aggressively on AI in H1 are the first to be discounted
