item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-cn38ff4a-全球流动性见顶-上半年越激进砸-ai-的公司-越先被折价/
item.description: A rising market needs new money to keep buying. Global liquidity is already showing signs of peaking, and the companies that invested most aggressively in AI in the first half are shifting from being rewarded to being discounted.
item.content:encoded:
A rising market needs new money to keep buying. Global liquidity is already showing signs of peaking, and the companies that invested most aggressively in AI in the first half are shifting from being rewarded to being discounted.

It puts US AI capex, Hong Kong IPO subscriptions and household balance sheets on the same funding chain — a macro framework that does not treat AI as a panacea.

0:33 A low IPO break rate is not a good signal
Do not read Hong Kong's low first-day break rate as a strengthening market. In the first half of this year the break rate was only in the teens, far below the roughly fifty-fifty level normal under a market-based mechanism — meaning the money subscribing to new listings is mainly short-term speculative arbitrage, not long-term investors. Recently the supply of listed companies has shrunk and a subscription-related fund blew up, yet the two most recent listings still broke issue, showing that temporary supply-side control has not fixed the underlying problem: Hong Kong faces the same peak in liquidity.

12:07 The more aggressive on AI, the sooner punished
Market attitude reversed within a single quarter. Before Q1, the capital market rewarded aggression: the louder the AI CapEx, the higher the valuation. By the time half-year reports were disclosed in late July, any large internet company that had made aggressive capex in the first half — especially those that burned through free cash flow — was discounted, and even Google was not exempt. Q2 was precisely the quarter of maximum FOMO across the whole supply chain, with everyone rushing to spend before prices rose, and inventory still able to hold up gross margins; by Q3, when inventory is exhausted and price increases feed back in, the negatives will show up together.

15:54 Nvidia is closer to Cisco in 2000
Nvidia's earnings look good, but its cash flow is changing shape. Before the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, Cisco rolled out rent-to-buy to help customers finance purchases, pulling future revenue forward into reported sales; Nvidia is now pushing rent-to-buy as well. Free cash flow in the report halved quarter on quarter, and receivables on the books are far above historical levels — which is suspected to be partly tied to the credit enhancement and collection structure that rent-to-buy brings. Nvidia may therefore have reached the stage where it needs more aggressive financial engineering to sustain capital-market expectations, a position similar to Cisco's back then.

33:21 Primary-market money is bullets from three years ago
The answer lies in when the funds raised. The money being deployed into AI and robotics from H2 2025 through H1 2026 comes mainly from funds raised at the 2020-2022 market peak; through 2023-2025 they barely invested, until they saw state capital placing bets when no one dared and making the most money — the stories of ChangXin and ChangCun, the two large models and the two big chip companies stirred up market-based capital, and the mood became: copy the state capital's homework. So this is not a rational long-term incremental wave; it looks more like a delayed emotional release.

47:31 Property policy detaches households from the funding chain
The key to recent real estate policy is not bailing out developers but pulling households out of the old financing loop. Buying a pre-sale home used to mean the household played the role of financier in the investment-driven chain: pay first, receive the home later; by pushing the chain toward a market-based model, buyers get completed homes and bear only the consumer role, with risk reset back onto developers and financing institutions. The policy was timed for when prices were near the bottom in order to first stabilise the denominator on the asset side, avoiding panic from dismantling the chain during a decline. Japan after the 1990s and the consolidation of China's coal and mining industries both followed similar paths.

1:01:34 A slow bull is not a slogan, it is chip structure
A slow bull does not come from shouting; it comes from layering market chips by duration: at the bottom, low-valuation high-dividend blue chips taken up by insurers as long money that rarely trades; above that, mutual funds and index funds, performing a quasi-stabilisation function; above that, China Securities Finance and Central Huijin adjusting the index; and only at the top, retail, private funds and active managers. The new insurance rules require liabilities and assets to match on duration, yield and liquidity — institutionally ensuring long money invests long, medium money medium, short money short: you are not allowed to take ordinary people's short money and put it into ten-year illiquid assets.

1:22:49 Crises get bigger with each rescue, bubbles at least one and a half
After the dollar left gold in 1971, global central banks grew ever more accustomed to intervening directly in crises by printing money, and each time faster than the last. The quantitative easing after 2008 should have been cleared out in a rate-hiking cycle, but political intervention cut it short, and then COVID hit in 2020, so a bigger wave of easing was layered on before the previous bubble had dissipated — at least one and a half bubbles accumulated by today. Central bank governors have learned to print more money the moment a crisis appears, and the endogenous result is inflation, rising financial assets and widening wealth inequality all at once. As long as the bubble is not allowed to clear, the world may face a form of long-term stagflation.

item.title: Central Banks Won't Kill the $100 Bill: It's a $2.5 Trillion Interest-Free Loan
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-oddlots-央行不愿废除百元美钞-那是一笔-2-5-万亿无息贷款/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-oddlots-央行不愿废除百元美钞-那是一笔-2-5-万亿无息贷款/
item.description: Cash use keeps falling, yet currency in circulation keeps hitting records. Central banks have an incentive to keep printing $100 bills: the money is effectively a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the U.S. government, and the price is convenience for money launderers worldwide.
item.content:encoded:
Cash use keeps falling, yet currency in circulation keeps hitting records. Central banks have an incentive to keep printing $100 bills: the money is effectively a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the U.S. government, and the price is convenience for money launderers worldwide.

It strips money laundering back from "bank wires" to watches, tractors, casino chips and VAT loopholes, and explains why central banks can't bear to kill the $100 bill.

5:09 The scale of money laundering hasn't changed in thirty years
The most commonly used estimate of money laundering is 2% to 5% of global GDP a year, which at today's roughly $100 trillion GDP is $2 trillion to $5 trillion. That number comes from a rough estimate by former IMF managing director Michel Camdessus in the late 1990s, and nobody has come up with a better answer since. Oliver warns that the more alarming fact is that this ratio hasn't moved in thirty years: decades of anti-money-laundering action have not shrunk the criminal economy, only barely held it back from growing faster than the overall economy.

9:10 Banks spend $200 billion a year on AML for near-zero effect
When banks complain that KYC is too expensive, it isn't just whining. The U.S. passed the Bank Secrecy Act in 1970, and in 1989 the FATF turned anti-money-laundering into a global norm, forcing banks to hire compliance teams and install AI monitoring software. LexisNexis estimates global AML compliance costs about $200 billion a year, enough to solve world hunger and provide clean water to everyone. Yet the system generates enormous numbers of suspicious activity reports every year, and launderers still run ahead of regulators. The problem isn't that banks aren't trying; it's that the whole system is expensive, weakly feedback-driven, and almost nobody is accountable for outcomes.

12:14 Trade-based laundering is an order of magnitude bigger than cash smuggling
Cash smuggling makes laundering inside the banking system look small, but the bigger chunk never touches money at all: value is hidden in goods. About $25 billion in cash flows into Mexico each year, while John Deere and Caterpillar farm equipment exported from the U.S. becomes the consideration cartels get back; European luxury goods flow to China, drugs and goods flow back toward China, and the triangle is settled with misinvoiced paperwork. Global Financial Integrity estimates this kind of trade-based laundering at about $1 trillion a year. A million-dollar watch on your wrist through customs is far easier than moving a million in cash.

17:18 The Vancouver model: Chinese cash demand meets cartel supply
Each person in China has only a $50,000 annual foreign-exchange quota, yet wealthy Chinese have plenty of demand to spend abroad. The Vancouver model matches that demand with the dollar cash supply from drug cartels: bags of cash outside Canadian casinos are handed to Chinese gamblers, the money is lost at the tables, and the gamblers owe gambling debts; that debt is offset on the other end in China by an RMB transaction and by drug sales that follow. Looked at as just the gambling, it looks like a loss; looked at across the whole chain, it is a triangular settlement that simultaneously repatriates cartel money and moves Chinese capital out. The model later spread worldwide, with luxury goods, consumer goods and drugs all serving as vehicles for moving value.

23:25 A VAT loophole lets the same goods extract 20% over and over
Zero-rated cross-border transactions in the EU were meant to keep national tax authorities from having to audit each other, but they became an ATM: goods entering the UK from Ireland don't owe VAT, and when sold to a related shell company 20% is added; that shell company re-exports the goods back to Ireland and can claim a 20% refund from UK tax authorities on VAT it never paid. Round and round it goes, hence carousel fraud. The UK once largely suppressed it with a multi-agency crackdown, and the fraudsters then moved to continental Europe, where it now runs about €50 billion a year, spreading from Lithuania all the way to Portugal. Criminal organizations have no ceiling on cooperation: the more they cooperate, the bigger they get.

27:27 Nobody uses cash, yet central banks are printing record banknotes
In the digital-payments era, cash transactions are down to about 9% in the UK and about 13% in the U.S., so by ordinary logic the supply of paper money should be shrinking. After Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey raised the banknote paradox in 2009, the phenomenon only intensified: the value of UK banknotes in circulation doubled, and the U.S. is near $2.5 trillion. Central banks blaming it on "store of value" doesn't hold up — surveys show the average American adult carries only a bit over $400, while per-capita U.S. currency in circulation works out to more than $7,000. The Fed estimates about 65% of U.S. banknotes are abroad, but that just pushes the question past the border: nobody knows whose hands these bills are actually sitting in.

32:31 The $100 bill is a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the government
Seigniorage can't simply be understood as the profit from printing money: a $100 bill costs 9 cents, but it isn't "sold" to you — you can always exchange it back for goods at face value, so cash held by the public is essentially an interest-free loan. With nearly $2.5 trillion in U.S. currency in circulation, the U.S. government gets interest-free funding equal to about 6% of the national debt; federal interest payments are now about 19% of the budget, and if that $2.5 trillion also had to pay interest, you'd add roughly another percentage point. That is exactly why central banks don't want to hear anyone discuss abolishing cash.

47:51 AML incentives are inverted: the more reports, the less crime gets policed
Suspicious activity reports were born to be real-time intelligence for law enforcement, but reality is the exact opposite: banks hire thousands of compliance officers to fill out reports, law enforcement has no resources to read them, and most reports fall into a black hole; a bank that misses one can face billion-dollar fines, while doing it right earns no reward. Side effects include debanking — large numbers of people who come under suspicion, many of them Muslim, get cut off by financial institutions. The guest's solution isn't to hire more compliance officers but to generate fewer reports, actually read them, and genuinely prosecute financial criminals, raising the cost of money laundering instead of drowning everyone in paperwork.

item.title: Russia Is Stuck in Ukraine, but It Still Has Room to Open a New Front Against NATO
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-hiddenforces-俄罗斯陷在乌克兰-仍有余力对北约开新战线/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-hiddenforces-俄罗斯陷在乌克兰-仍有余力对北约开新战线/
item.description: Russia has not won in Ukraine, but its war of attrition has forged the world's most advanced drone-infantry combat experience; the guest argues it has ample capacity to launch a limited probe against NATO, and the window is in the final phase of Trump's term.
item.content:encoded:
Russia has not won in Ukraine, but its war of attrition has forged the world's most advanced drone-infantry combat experience; the guest argues it has ample capacity to launch a limited probe against NATO, and the window is in the final phase of Trump's term.

The guest is the Wall Street Journal's chief diplomatic correspondent and was in Kyiv on the day of the 2022 invasion; his judgments on Russian military capability and Europe's fractures are far more concrete than those of TV commentators.

19:16 Trump's anti-Europe talk may be taken literally by Putin
Everyone is speculating about whether John Ratcliffe's secret trip to Russia was there to negotiate terms. The guest's read is that the visit looks more like carrying a message to Moscow on Trump's behalf: don't take those on-air remarks about America abandoning Europe seriously — if Russia invades Lithuania, Estonia or Finland, the US will send troops. The reasoning is that Moscow is bogged down in a war of attrition in Ukraine and badly needs to cut off European support for Ukraine, so escalating with a probe against NATO is one option, and Trump's earlier statements — that Europe is a bunch of freeloaders — gave Putin room to misread, hence the need for a dedicated trip to make the red line clear. One caveat: the guest does not have intelligence from inside that room; he is explaining why the account is entirely plausible, not confirming it.

21:27 Russia's army isn't exhausted — it can still open a limited front
Russia has been unable to take Ukraine for a long time — does that mean it cannot open another front? The guest's answer is blunt: it can absolutely open a limited front — not tanks rolling across Poland to Paris, but something in the Baltic direction, such as blockading the narrow land corridor of the Suwalki Gap. He says the Russian and Ukrainian armies are the only two in the world today that fight modern drone-infantry warfare as a daily routine. The story of a 20-person Ukrainian drone team destroying an entire traditional battalion is widely told, but the Russian military has the same technology in hand: 20 Russians can likewise wipe out a NATO battalion that has not trained against drones. Outsiders assume Russia grows weaker the longer it fights, and overlook that it is also one of the parties being tempered by this technological revolution.

22:31 NATO might not even rescue Lithuania from Poland
A war game designed to simulate a Russian invasion of Lithuania led the guest to a deeply unsettling conclusion: even Poland did not send troops to save Lithuania, let alone other allies. The reason is not a lack of military capability but the speed of Russian advance, combined with the shadow of nuclear deterrence, which would leave allies hesitating over whether to enter and produce a chain of waiting and watching. The guest says Moscow factors exactly this into its options. He also cautions that this is not quite the same as before 2022 — back then, over a hundred thousand Russian troops could be clearly seen massing on the German and Belarusian borders, and there is no such material preparation now. So the most immediate escalation may not be a conventional invasion but small, ambiguous, deniable attacks — hitting a warehouse or a drone first.

23:40 Russia is already probing NATO's limits with drones
At this stage, with no sign of a massed army on the border, Russia still holds a set of low-cost, low-attribution options: a limited strike on a NATO warehouse near Poland or Romania, or a provocation using a captured Ukrainian drone modified for the purpose, then watching whether NATO splits and whether the US steps in. The guest notes this kind of probing is already underway — an armed drone attacked a Ukrainian aircraft parked at Leipzig airport in Germany, and only a drone malfunction prevented casualties; Russian risk-taking is steadily rising, and the West has yet to give a serious response. The senior European officers he speaks with all believe the most dangerous window is the next one to two years, roughly falling in the final phase of Trump's term — the Kremlin will want to act before the US might let go.

27:53 Putin wants Ukraine disarmed, not a ceasefire
Would Putin accept an honorable ceasefire deal? The guest's view is that you only need to look at what is put on the table: Russia has consistently demanded not just territory but a cap on the size of Ukraine's army, limits on the types of weapons it may hold, and a cutoff of Western military aid to Ukraine. In his words, the goal is to leave Ukraine unable to defend itself; not neutral, but emasculated, so that it cannot rise again in the next stage of the war — a year, five years or ten years from now. Putin signed Minsk-1 and Minsk-2, and violated both. So the guest quotes the summary of Ukraine's former foreign minister: this war will end in one of only two ways — the end of Ukraine, or the end of the Russian imperial project. Waiting for the other side to change its mind is not on the menu.

31:08 Street protests can decide the fate of a wartime cabinet
Kyiv's recent personnel earthquake looks on the surface like an anti-corruption storm, but the key mechanism lies elsewhere: elections are frozen in wartime, and the president's legitimacy rests on street support as its only ballast. Zelensky initially fired Defense Minister Fedorov, who was driving drone innovation, because he needed the backing of Commander-in-Chief Syrskyi; after Fedorov was dismissed, Kyiv elites took to the streets, and the protests, small as they were, were enough to make the president reverse course — he removed Syrskyi, brought in a younger general more popular with the front line, and appointed a defense minister with a veteran intelligence background acceptable to all sides. Ukraine's independent anti-corruption bodies can still pursue people in the president's innermost circle, and when Zelensky tried to amend the law to bring that body under his control, he backed down within a week under street pressure. When elections are absent, the square equals the ballot.

38:37 Resistance comes from memory, not heroism
Summing up Ukrainian perseverance as patriotic heroism misses what actually drives them. The guest says that after Russian troops take a Ukrainian town, one of the first things they often do is send bulldozers to tear down monuments to the victims of the 1930s famine — what they want to erase is a memory. Russian state television talks about how to re-educate Ukrainians, to make them forget their language and culture and become Russians. Around World War II, the Soviets carried out a systematic purge of Ukraine's cultural elite, and in the guest's childhood he had no idea those writers existed, because collective memory had been wiped out. Ukrainians today are almost all descendants of survivors of that meat grinder, carrying the trauma in their bodies; it is the fear of never again that makes them prefer to die on the battlefield rather than return to that life.

45:59 Half a million veterans held off the first collapse
On the night of February 23, 2022, most people in Kyiv still did not believe there would be a war; the guest remembers knowing from his experience in Kabul and Baghdad that impossible can flip overnight, but ordinary Ukrainians had no such reference point. What really kept the country from collapsing in the first days was eight years of war in the Donbas: that fighting was far from Kyiv, but it produced roughly 500,000 Ukrainians who had traded blows with the Russian army, and volunteer organizations that evolved into a flexible, aggressive force. The psychological threshold had already been crossed in the Donbas — we know what they look like, we know how to fight them. Because of that experience, the swift collapse Putin expected did not happen, and the West's widespread expectations were wrong too.

item.title: A Child Hitting, Biting or Kicking Isn't Misbehaving — They're Reclaiming Bodily Autonomy
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-parentmojo-孩子打咬踢不是坏行为-是在夺回身体自主权/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-parentmojo-孩子打咬踢不是坏行为-是在夺回身体自主权/
item.description: Stop asking how to make the hitting stop. For a three- or four-year-old, hitting, biting and kicking are often the only tool left to shout "I have no say" after adults have taken control of nearly everything their body does — give some choice back, and the behavior shrinks.
item.content:encoded:
Stop asking how to make the hitting stop. For a three- or four-year-old, hitting, biting and kicking are often the only tool left to shout "I have no say" after adults have taken control of nearly everything their body does — give some choice back, and the behavior shrinks.

Most approaches restate "no hitting" and add punishment, never touching the need that precedes the behavior. This episode treats aggression as a need signal, and models the scripts and cases for negotiating with teachers.

4:21 A child who hits is shouting that they can't control their body
Preschool is often the first place a child is controlled in nearly every bodily arrangement by an adult other than a parent: where to sit, how to sit, when to speak and when to move. For the previous three years, they could roughly decide when to run and when to use the toilet. Sitting on a rug for 20 minutes without moving is a real deprivation of autonomy; and a three- or four-year-old has no language to assert "my body is mine to decide," so hitting and kicking become one of the few tools still available. So when the call home comes, don't rush to lecture "hands to yourself" — ask instead: how much say did this child have over their own life before this, and what small piece of it can be handed back now.

6:42 Kindergarten readiness is really obedience training
Teachers often say a given preschool has a high share of kindergarten-ready children, and the core definition of that readiness is compliance: sit still when the teacher says sit still, even mid-task, even when the body is already overloaded. Parents fear that if the child doesn't comply now, they won't get into a good elementary school, college, a good life. But the price the child pays for that definition is learning to suppress the feeling of "what I need right now." Teachers aren't villains either — they too need to feel competent, to keep children safe, to conserve energy, and even to enjoy some power; many entered education precisely to repair their own childhood wounds, yet only know the power-over style of relationship. Seeing both sides' situations is what opens room to negotiate.

9:24 We give ourselves accommodations and deny them to children
If an adult feels overloaded at a party, they arrive early, leave early, hide in a quiet room, even wear noise-cancelling earplugs — we consider this perfectly natural. Point the camera at a child, though, and apart from routines like extra exam time, we immediately worry that "too much accommodation will spoil them, they'll never survive the real world." The truth is that adults grant themselves far more accommodation than they allow children. The source offers a concrete image: an adult stronger than you unceremoniously carries you out of the quiet room back to the center of the loud party — swap in an adult and you instantly see it as a violation of bodily autonomy; when it happens to a child we look right past it.

12:11 The repair point is before the behavior, not the behavior itself
Repeating "hitting is not okay" doesn't work, because that isn't knowledge the child is missing. You need a different set of questions: what happened in the seconds before this bite? What happened earlier in the day? Is there a move or a new baby in the child's life? A sensory-overloaded child who gets jostled in line will melt down, so let them stand at the front, the back, or outside the line; a child who struggles with transitions needs a few minutes' warning. The adult analogy: when your partner snaps at you for no reason at night, it's usually not about that sentence but about the morning's argument, lost sleep, and a pile of stress. If they then tossed off "your attitude needs work," you'd blow up too — yet we routinely do only the latter to children.

15:10 Talking to the teacher: don't assign blame, hear what the "no" protects
Telling a teacher "please change what you're doing" will almost certainly hit a wall. The safer opening is to drop judgment and reconstruct the facts: don't look for who's responsible, just ask what actually happened; and include family changes, which are context the teacher can't see. Once you know whether the child's trigger is sensory or autonomy, extend empathy to the three things behind the teacher: competence, the child's safety, and the energy saved by getting a breather. The request must land on a concrete, doable change, like "can the child sit on a ball outside the circle." If the teacher refuses, the key isn't the refusal but what need that "no" is still protecting, and finding a different approach that satisfies both sides.

16:07 A naptime conflict, cleanly taken apart
Jen's daughter Carys, at three, couldn't nap, and the teacher wanted her to lie down; she was bored and frustrated — her need was to play. The teacher had two needs: state rules required offering a nap, and naptime was the teacher's own rest period. The solution they found was to move her mat to a slightly separated corner, where she could quietly play with soft toys that wouldn't roll, and the teacher could see her through the window from the break room. The child kept her right to free play, the teacher kept the rule and her rest, and Jen escaped the no-win cycle of incident reports. This segment shows that "negotiating by need" isn't empty talk: everyone gives a little, but everyone's core need is held.

17:53 Every method comes down to one question in the end
Compress all of the above into a single line: stop asking "how do I make the hitting stop," and ask "what need is this behavior communicating?" Hitting, biting and kicking are only surface signals; the real message may be "I need sensory relief" or "I need some say over my own body." Once the need is correctly named, a path to meeting it can be designed; and it is almost always the adult who changes the environment, because changing how the adult shows up is far easier than changing the child.

item.title: The Thai Flood That Wrecked the Hard Disk Drive Industry: The Biggest Factory Fell, the Number Two Took the Throne
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-asianometry-泰国洪水重创硬盘业-最大的厂跌倒-老二捡了王座/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-asianometry-泰国洪水重创硬盘业-最大的厂跌倒-老二捡了王座/
item.description: One flood in Thailand redrew the hard drive rankings: Western Digital's shipments fell 51% quarter over quarter, Seagate's fell only 8%, and Seagate overtook it to take the top spot.
item.content:encoded:
One flood in Thailand redrew the hard drive rankings: Western Digital's shipments fell 51% quarter over quarter, Seagate's fell only 8%, and Seagate overtook it to take the top spot.

What are the risks of geographic concentration in a manufacturing supply chain? This flood is a complete case study — industrial estate siting, zero inventory and a single point of failure all detonating at once.

6:13 Flood walls gave the hard drive makers a false sense of security
The industrial estates were built on river floodplain converted from rice paddies north of Bangkok. For flood protection, developers installed ring levees up to two metres high, secondary wave walls, pumps and drainage systems; the parks quickly grew into small cities with their own housing and shops. But this engineering may have misled everyone. When the real flood season arrived in 2011, seven industrial parks were inundated within two weeks. Research later suspected that precisely this kind of seemingly complete infrastructure created a false confidence — the belief that even if it rained, everything would be fine. In other words, what the manufacturers bought was not safety, but an illusion about risk.

8:24 Reservoir releases were not the culprit; local rainfall was
After the flood, dam managers were blamed for releasing water too late, with criticism focused on favouring farmers and rice-corruption allegations. But the research does not support that blame. A 2023 simulation ran 17 scenarios swapping the release strategies of two dams, and concluded that even with perfect foresight of subsequent rainfall, the flooded area could have been reduced by at most 3.68%. Another 2020 study examined hydrological station data along the Chao Phraya River and found that in one low-lying disaster area, less than 30% of the floodwater came from the river, while 73.7% came from local rainfall. In other words, the water mainly fell directly on the disaster area's head; reservoir decisions cannot carry that blame.

9:25 Why Seagate stalled even though it wasn't flooded
Seagate's factories in the north at Korat were basically fine, but production stopped anyway — because seven of its top ten suppliers were underwater. The typical case was Japan's Nidec, which makes spindle motors for hard drives and shut down production outright after two of its plants flooded. The hard drive supply chain interlocks layer by layer: however safe the assembly line, if the motors don't come, the whole line stops. Seagate held its quarterly shipment decline to 8% by quickly qualifying new suppliers, modifying designs to reduce complexity, and negotiating payment terms with suppliers. In the same year, Western Digital's core plant took on water 1.8 metres deep, and its quarterly shipments fell 51%. The difference between the two was not whose building was taller, but whose underlying supply chain could route around the break faster.

12:34 Zero inventory amplified the flood into a global shortage
Before the flood hit, the hard drive industry had just completed a round of consolidation: Western Digital announced in March 2011 that it would acquire Hitachi's hard drive business, and a month later Seagate announced it would acquire Samsung, barely bringing supply and demand back into balance. Precisely because there was no surplus inventory to draw down, the shock was multiplied. Tom Coughlin estimated that fourth-quarter 2011 hard drive demand was about 180 million units, while actual production was only 110 million to 120 million; and the flood happened to hit the Christmas shopping season. Retail immediately marked up spot prices by 20% to 40%, and a 1TB drive at Taipei's Guanghua Market went from NT$1,750 to over NT$3,000. Even Intel admitted in December that Q4 revenue would be about $1 billion short of expectations because of the hard drive shortage. A local flood, transmitted through zero inventory, became a global shortage just like that.

15:41 The water receded, but hard drive prices didn't fall for two years
The water receded, but the shortage did not end quickly. Hard drive availability only returned to pre-disaster levels about nine months later; retail prices fell back more slowly — hard drive prices on Newegg did not drop back to pre-disaster levels until April 2013. Backblaze did the math from its own purchasing records: in September 2011 the cost per GB was $0.044, and it would take until September 2013 to return to that level again. Why is it easy to raise prices and hard to cut them? The author lists several interpretations: the ecosystem recovered more slowly than expected, the two giants' 2011 acquisitions brought extra costs, tablets caused PC hard drive demand to fall permanently, and a more cynical guess — after Seagate and Western Digital acquired their second-tier rivals, only three major manufacturers remained in the whole industry, making prices easier to ‘stabilise’, or in his own word: cartelize. As for which one is the truth, he does not conclude.

18:47 The flooded giant chose to stay and keep building walls
Western Digital's post-disaster choice is telling: it did not retreat, it doubled down on defences. WD and the Bang Pa-in estate owner built an 11-kilometre flood wall along the estate, and WD added a 6-metre-high inner wall around its factory; to add redundancy to its supply chain, in December 2011 it announced a new slider fab in Malaysia. A survey of 50 directly affected Japanese companies showed that nearly 80% decided to stay in Thailand. The reasons are not hard to understand: ready-made estates, supporting infrastructure and skilled workers are hard to pack up and take away. Thailand has since suffered several more rounds of major flooding, especially in the 2020s when it happened almost every year; in November of the most recent year it even rained in what was billed as a ‘once in 300 years’ event, but these estates have held out so far. Whether stronger defences will be needed in future can only be tested by the next big flood.

item.title: AI designs viruses that infect bacteria, but only 5% of the time
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-twiv-ai-设计出能感染细菌的病毒-但成功率仅-5/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-twiv-ai-设计出能感染细菌的病毒-但成功率仅-5/
item.description: For the first time, AI designed a complete viral genome from scratch that can infect bacteria; experimental validation puts the success rate at about 5%, nowhere near as omnipotent as the media suggests.
item.content:encoded:
For the first time, AI designed a complete viral genome from scratch that can infect bacteria; experimental validation puts the success rate at about 5%, nowhere near as omnipotent as the media suggests.

This episode takes apart the success rate of AI-made viruses, compensatory mutations and biosafety rhetoric, and also demonstrates how an observational vaccine study can be falsified by an E-value.

12:43 A vaccine switch as a natural control
The trap in "healthy vaccinee bias" is that vaccinated people tend to pay more attention to their own health than unvaccinated people, so comparing the two groups mistakes lifestyle differences for vaccine effects. This study exploits the moment in 2017 when the US shingles vaccine switched wholesale from Zostavax to Shingrix: those vaccinated before the policy switch got the old vaccine, those after got the new one, and both groups were people who actively sought vaccination, so in theory the bias is erased. It is still not a randomised trial, however — unmeasured factors such as socioeconomic status, smoking and diet could still be unbalanced between the two groups, so it counts only as a quasi-experiment.

15:47 Weak confounding alone can overturn a vaccine benefit
How strong would unmeasured confounding have to be to overturn an observational conclusion? That is what the E-value measures. The E-value for this vaccine study is only 1.42, almost hugging 1, meaning a confounder that is not even very strong but is associated with both "which vaccine was received" and "cardiovascular outcomes" could explain away the observed risk reduction. An E-value needs to reach 3.4 or even 5 for a conclusion to count as solid; 1.42 is far from robust. The authors themselves admit that a randomised clinical trial is needed to confirm it, and that this observation cannot be treated as evidence.

38:13 AI produces a functional viral genome for the first time
The researchers took the genomic language models EVO1 and EVO2 and had them write phage genomes: first the models read massive public DNA sequence data, then they were fine-tuned on PhiX174 to generate thousands of candidate sequences. Back in the lab, only about 5% of the products could actually infect E. coli — the first time AI has designed a complete genome from scratch that was proven functional. If the media summarises this as "AI directly made a virus", it misses a key point: the model has only ever seen sequences, with no experimental annotation telling it which base does what, and the 5% hit rate shows how ignorant it still is about how sequence determines function.

44:37 The origin of replication is the model's most conserved memory
The prompt given to the model needed only the first 4 to 9 nucleotides of the PhiX174 genome for the accuracy of the output to rise markedly. The authors found that this unremarkable stretch is part of the origin of replication, and it was 100% conserved across every genome the model generated. It works like a password meaning "I am a real virus": the model treats the origin of replication as a core that must be locked down, and only dares to let other positions evolve. That also explains why such a short prompt works — what matters is not the prompt's length but whether it hits a functional pressure point.

56:55 AI swaps one gene and adds 58 mutations itself
The design idea behind EVO36 was not to rewrite the whole thing but to swap genes: replace PhiX174's J gene with the shorter J protein from phage G4. When humans did the same transplant by hand in the past, the product could not infect; but the AI's EVO36 infects normally, because it accumulated an extra 58 mutations across the genome. These look like compensatory mutations that let the foreign J protein re-adapt to its new environment. Humans might not think to touch 58 positions at once, and this is exactly where a generative model exceeds the reach of single-point editing.

1:00:15 Mixed phages specifically target drug-resistant bacteria
Natural PhiX174 hits a wall against already-resistant bacteria and cannot break through even after five passages; a mix of 16 AI-synthesised phages infected the originally resistant strain within one or two generations. Resistance is not broken by any single phage but by several synthetic phages recombining with each other and accumulating new mutations during replication, finally breaking the barrier through collective action. The result suggests that phage therapy should not bet on a single strain but should send in a cocktail of multiple synthetic phages.

1:07:29 Don't call AI-made viruses an urgent threat
For that study generating PhiX174, a contemporaneous commentary used the word "urgent" to describe its biosafety implications. Vincent pushed back on that wording directly on the show: the authors had already shown through reproducible experiments that this kind of research can be done safely, so what is needed is not an alarm bell but the start of building a safety framework. He also stressed that reconstructing a virus is not science fiction as long as you have enough sequence — precisely why a framework is needed rather than fearmongering.

1:35:53 Not getting vaccinated is often just not knowing
Discussing the unvaccinated population, the article raises an often overlooked mechanism: some people do not get vaccinated not out of religious or ideological opposition but because they simply do not know they should. Treating vaccine hesitancy uniformly as a "matter of faith" gets the policy response wrong — for this group the key is not debate or persuasion but reaching them with information so they first know the vaccine exists.

item.title: Sports Betting Has Infiltrated Gen Z, and the Regulatory Risk Is Underestimated
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-excessreturns-体育博彩渗透z世代-金融监管风险被低估/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-excessreturns-体育博彩渗透z世代-金融监管风险被低估/
item.description: Sports betting is becoming part of Gen Z's financial strategy. Slow losses are harder to recover from than one big blowup, and it sits on the same platform as financial products. The future regulatory risk is widely underestimated.
item.content:encoded:
Sports betting is becoming part of Gen Z's financial strategy. Slow losses are harder to recover from than one big blowup, and it sits on the same platform as financial products. The future regulatory risk is widely underestimated.

A multi-angle look at the hidden dangers of financialised gambling, from wealth management and market structure to regulation, with forward-looking value for understanding how the younger generation invests and where policy may change.

3:06 Gen Z treats betting as a financial strategy
A Betterment survey shows 26% of Gen Z investors see sports betting as part of their long-term financial strategy; in a CNBC survey, 52% of Gen Z investors moved money out of investments into sports betting over the past year. These numbers match Dave's experience with younger clients. Betting has seeped into every layer of Gen Z, and wealth management has to face it.

11:09 Slow losses are harder to recover from than a blowup
The insidious thing about sports betting is that there is rarely a dramatic blowup. Instead there is a steady drip of small losses: betting hundreds of baseball games over a summer, slowly losing 10% a week, occasionally winning 20% and feeling good, round and round. That erosive financial despair is harder to recover from than one big mistake. It amounts to a chronic tax on numeracy.

17:14 Regulatory risk is widely underestimated
Dave argues most people ignore regulatory risk because they assume regulators respond to catastrophic events. More likely, some future administration or state regulator suddenly says "enough." He points to Florida and Texas banning speed cameras first, showing how unpredictable regulatory moves are. Companies that depend on the current regulatory environment need to be on guard.

21:14 Leveraged ETF products raise market-structure worries
In the same week, South Korea set strict investor-education thresholds for 2x leveraged products, Japan explicitly rejected single-stock leverage, and the US saw a filing for a 2x leveraged product that resets hourly. What worries Dave more is that the new ETF tries to hedge gambling risk using the futures market, but that futures market does not exist until the ETF has assets. That inverts the order and could divert resources from important financial participants who stabilise oil prices.

25:20 Big Tech earnings show financial gimmicks
Cameron notes that Nvidia extended receivables to help customers, while hyperscaler customers extended payables to flatter free cash flow; Microsoft reclassified some capex into investing cash flow, lowering its capex guidance; activity inside SPVs does not show up on the statements. These financial gimmicks are common at cycle peaks. If the fundamentals were good, there would be no need for them.

29:24 Less disclosure worsens information asymmetry
Cameron opposes moving earnings to a semi-annual schedule with reduced disclosure, arguing it worsens information asymmetry, benefits institutions with the resources to assemble information through the mosaic effect, and makes markets less efficient. He also points to regulatory trends such as overturning the Chevron doctrine, all of which concentrate power at the top and work against innovation and competition.

38:27 The line between cultural appropriation and acceptance
Cameron criticises Urban Outfitters for selling Nirvana tie-dye sweatpants to 12-year-olds, calling it a lack of respect for the context. Dave thinks it may be a gateway to the music: even if a kid starts out liking only the smiley face, it could lead them to listen to Heart-Shaped Box. The argument reflects the tension between gatekeeping and openness in how culture spreads.

47:35 Finding role models as an adult means accepting imperfection
Dave shares the story of Keith Morris defusing a conflict at a Circle Jerks show, which sparks a discussion about role models. Cameron notes that as people age they learn to appreciate others' strengths while accepting their flaws, just as they do with their parents, taking the good and leaving the rest. Dave admits he cannot find a living role model because he knows no one is perfect.

item.title: Ion Drives: Slow Push, and the Win in the Space Race
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-isaacarthur-离子推进-慢慢推-反而赢下太空竞速/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-isaacarthur-离子推进-慢慢推-反而赢下太空竞速/
item.description: A rocket isn't necessarily better the more violent it is. An ion engine's thrust is as light as a sheet of paper, yet it can run for years on end, accumulating speeds chemical rockets can't reach on a tiny amount of propellant — and becoming the workhorse of space logistics.
item.content:encoded:
A rocket isn't necessarily better the more violent it is. An ion engine's thrust is as light as a sheet of paper, yet it can run for years on end, accumulating speeds chemical rockets can't reach on a tiny amount of propellant — and becoming the workhorse of space logistics.

This episode covers ion propulsion's principles, limits and applications in full — suited to anyone who wants a systematic understanding of why electric propulsion is now mainstream for deep space and satellites; those with no taste for engine detail can focus on the thrust and applications segments.

1:04 Ion propulsion wins on endurance
The rocket equation is cruel: to go faster you must throw away more mass, or throw it faster — but carrying more propellant makes the vehicle heavier, a tax-collector's loop. Chemical rockets use high thrust to leave Earth quickly, but their exhaust velocity is capped by the energy stored in chemical bonds. Ion propulsion takes another route: instead of burning fuel, it uses electric fields to accelerate a small number of charged particles to extremely high speeds and throw them out. The thrust is astonishingly small, yet it can persist for weeks, months, even years, ultimately accumulating a velocity change chemical rockets struggle to match.

4:04 Specific impulse and thrust can't both be had
Specific impulse measures how efficiently propellant is used; chemical rockets reach only a few hundred seconds, ion engines thousands. But that high efficiency rests on extremely low thrust: an ion engine can never lift off from the surface of Earth, the Moon or Mars — at most it can depart a small asteroid that an astronaut could jump off into space. It isn't physically impossible; it trades thrust for efficiency, and time for speed. Chemical rockets are sprinters, ion engines are marathoners.

6:07 Two mainstream forms of electric propulsion
The classic gridded ion thruster ionises propellant atoms and accelerates them out through charged grids — high efficiency, but the grids are continuously eroded. Hall thrusters use electromagnetic fields to ionise and accelerate propellant, with somewhat lower specific impulse but greater thrust and better suitability for satellites; they are the mainstay of modern electric propulsion. There are also micro electric-thruster systems for small satellites, and high-power plasma concepts — the core difference among these approaches ultimately comes down to how to obtain enough electrical power.

10:13 Why xenon is the default propellant
Propellant choice isn't intuitive: at the same accelerating voltage, helium ions fly fastest and xenon slowest, but thrust depends on momentum — mass times velocity — so helium looks tempting. Yet at the same power, a higher exhaust velocity actually means lower thrust; helium needs about 590 megajoules to ionise a kilogram, xenon only about 9 megajoules. Xenon is an inert gas that doesn't corrode the engine. It is today's high-end choice for ion propulsion, but costs about a thousand dollars per kilogram. Argon is far cheaper and is the industrial choice of the future.

18:20 Slow rockets are the bedrock of space logistics
Ion propulsion is especially suited to missions already in orbit: spiralling orbits up or down, rendezvousing with low-gravity small bodies. Humans are impatient cargo, but supplies — water, metal, parts, propellant — don't care about being shipped slowly. Future Mars plans or lunar bases can use chemical or nuclear thermal propulsion to move people fast, while ion engines deliver the cargo slowly ahead of time. Machines do the dull work; the history of civilisation is written in freighters, ships, railways, trucks and containers.

26:25 Longevity is the core requirement, not a bonus
An ion thruster must run continuously for thousands or even tens of thousands of hours; grids erode, cathodes fail, power processing units must survive years of operation. A chemical engine burns for only minutes, an ion engine for years — this isn't easier, it's a different direction in which things get hard. It also struggles to exploit the Oberth effect: a chemical rocket can burn hard and briefly at orbital perigee for a huge gain in orbital energy, while an ion engine's thrust is spread over months and loses that advantage for nothing.

30:26 Propellant isn't fuel, it's money
Propellant isn't just fuel; it is mass that must be launched, mined, processed, stored, transferred and protected. Every kilogram of propellant saved means more instruments, shielding, cargo and lifetime. The key of the early space age was whether you could reach space; the key of the next era is whether you can move around in space cheaply. Ion propulsion isn't enough to send people to Mars, but it may be the crucial tool for building space infrastructure — exploration gets the headlines, logistics builds civilisation.

31:26 Low-speed engines can build an interstellar civilisation
Today's ion engines cannot carry out interstellar flight within a human lifetime, but far-future electric propulsion — with megavolt or even gigavolt accelerators, enormous power systems and propellant measured in tonnes — would begin to approach an interstellar precursor vehicle. More crucially, even if ion engines never become interstellar drives, they remain key to building the infrastructure of an interstellar civilisation: before launching an interstellar ship, you need to build collectors, mines, fuel depots, telescope arrays, habitats and shipyards. These must be moved, assembled, maintained and resupplied, and ion propulsion may be the best choice for that slow work. It isn't the interstellar ship's engine itself; it is one of the engines that builds the civilisation, and then builds the interstellar ship.

item.title: Companies Are Becoming a Series of Loops: AI Can Reach the Peak, but Choosing the Next Mountain Still Takes a Human
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-lennys-公司变成一串自动循环-ai-能到坡顶-换山还得靠人/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-lennys-公司变成一串自动循环-ai-能到坡顶-换山还得靠人/
item.description: Companies are being rebuilt as a series of interlocking loops; loops can push the current business to a local maximum, but after the plateau, picking the next mountain still depends on human intuition.
item.content:encoded:
Companies are being rebuilt as a series of interlocking loops; loops can push the current business to a local maximum, but after the plateau, picking the next mountain still depends on human intuition.

A structural judgment from an a16z partner: companies will be rewritten by loops, and the biggest opportunity in consumer AI is joy, not efficiency. The takes are often counterintuitive — good for stress-testing your own product roadmap.

4:05 The AI era will not replicate winner-take-all
The AI era will not play out the way mobile internet did, with winner-take-all dynamics: network effects once pushed search and social toward one or two players, whereas today each layer of the AI stack has roughly 20 relevant participants. Two years ago everyone thought coding agents would end up with a single winner; now Claude Code, Codex, Lovable and Replit are all moving forward at once. Anish says the people at the frontier inside the labs believe what is actually happening is autocatalytic effects — using new technology to improve your own processes — rather than recursive self-improvement, so there will be no runaway winner that swallows everyone. The implication for founders: don't bet on a single full-stack giant; every layer (models, agents, interfaces) still has a long-term place.

10:08 CEOs want to build bigger companies, not fewer employees
Employees probably don't need to worry too much about being replaced by AI — not because the technology isn't strong enough, but because a CEO's incentive is growth, not shrinkage. Sundar doesn't want to run a more efficient $4 trillion company; he wants to build a $40 trillion company. A Google executive friend told Anish that the company isn't laying people off — it's using AI to compress a two-year roadmap into three months, and the hard problem has become "what do we add to the roadmap." When execution is no longer scarce, attention shifts from saving labor to finding new things to do for a bigger goal.

15:12 Companies will become loops, and the next step needs a human to set it
The shape of a company is shifting from a list of roles and departments into a cascade of loops: first the automation of an individual's workflow, then functional loops, then loops that cross business units, and ultimately loops running most of the company's operations. The loops themselves keep producing output, and that output becomes the input to the next layer of loops; some mechanism sends the signal back to the CEO — when to adjust the business entity, when the strategy should change. This machinery can help a company climb to a local maximum, but after the plateau it must rely on human intuition to do out-of-distribution thinking and put the organization at the foot of the next mountain. Asking AI to directly come up with a million-dollar idea often fails, because humans can set the right direction while AI is only responsible for sweeping along a given slope.

32:24 Users want to spend time, not save it
Silicon Valley defaults to AI's value being efficiency; Anish thinks that's a misjudgment: most people don't really want to save time, they want to spend it where it brings connection, love, progress and fun. The biggest products in history have always been entertainment and social, so AI's consumer opportunity is not "a few more minutes saved" but building loops that make people feel more connected, more loved, and feel progress or fun. He criticizes the last 40 years of technology for extending intelligence while barely extending the soul; fitting AI into these desires is a product design challenge, not a model capability challenge.

37:29 AI is decoupling skill from desire
Anish sees AI not just as a productivity tool but more like an emotional and spiritual interface — it can split "skill" and "desire" apart. People who want to make music are no longer blocked by "can't play piano"; people who want to write code don't have to first learn it to the point of being employable; personal identity is amplified as a result. He looks back at the high-risk environment of the 1950s-60s, which greatly stimulated human potential, and argues today's world is in a low-risk state; AI has a chance to pull GDP growth from 2% to 10-15% — provided it raises not the speed of a single step, but the scale of what a group dares to imagine.

1:04:42 Ideas that are too small now fail to get funded
Investment criteria have reversed within three years. In the past, if a project was too ambitious, funds would often say a $100 million seed round was absurd; today, looking at deals at a16z, the reverse standard has arrived — if an idea can still only be that small with AI's help, they simply don't invest. "Unbounded ambition" has become the core value for screening companies; Marc Andreessen's version is: we either go to the moon, or we leave a moon-sized crater.

1:09:48 Shipping something small every week is how you build product intuition
The most direct advice for product people is the old line: build more things. Find a project you tell no one about, the smaller the better, treat it as a "chassis," run each new model through it, ship the finished thing, discuss it with people — that's the path to building AI intuition. The cadence only needs to be one small release a week; going crazy isn't sustainable. Anish himself used Codex to make a Mother's Day slideshow for his wife: pulling material from texts and the photo album, scoring it automatically, and ending up with 20 pages reviewing their relationship, even digging up old texts from their first date. It's small, but work like this lets you taste AI's "moments of joy" again and again — once you've tasted it, you can't go back.

item.title: US Outposts Were Dangerous Bubbles: How the War on Terror Trapped Itself
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-05-chinatalk-美军哨所是危险气泡-反恐战争如何困住自己/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-05-chinatalk-美军哨所是危险气泡-反恐战争如何困住自己/
item.description: US outposts in Afghanistan were meant to protect villages, but became targets that drew in conflict. The harder they fought, the heavier they got, losing mobility until they were trapped by the fortresses they built.
item.content:encoded:
US outposts in Afghanistan were meant to protect villages, but became targets that drew in conflict. The harder they fought, the heavier they got, losing mobility until they were trapped by the fortresses they built.

Wesley Morgan served on the ground in Afghanistan and spent a decade researching the deep contradictions of the War on Terror: tactical success coexisting with strategic failure, worth pondering for anyone who follows war and organizations.

5:00 The outpost became a dangerous bubble
In the summer of 2010, Wesley Morgan went into Afghanistan's Pech Valley with the troops and found that US outposts meant to provide security for villages had in fact become ‘dangerous bubbles’ that drew conflict toward the villagers. Both the Americans and the enemy suffered few casualties; the real suffering was in the villages outside the outposts. That contrast set him asking: who built these outposts, why, and when — questions that eventually became his book The Hardest Place.

10:39 The US military grew heavier and dumber
From 2006 to 2010, US forces in eastern Afghanistan gradually lost flexibility and mobility, tethered to heavy outposts and MRAPs. In 2006 the 10th Mountain Division could still reach remote areas by pickup and ATV, but by 2010, because of the IED threat and top-down force-protection requirements, conventional units could barely get to those places and had to rely on special operations for offensive missions. That overextension meant follow-on units could not sustain the earlier reach.

12:51 Two ODA teams: restraint and recklessness
In 2004, two Green Beret ODA teams deployed to the Pech Valley in succession. The first, from the Utah National Guard's 19th Special Forces Group, used an ‘inkblot’ approach, trying to build secure zones around district centers, and refused to enter the Korengal Valley because they sensed something there was luring them in. The second, from the 3rd Special Forces Group at Fort Bragg, was eager to get into the Korengal looking for a fight, got entangled in a local tribal timber dispute, was used as muscle by one faction, and started the Korengal ‘snowball’ that eventually became a fierce battlefield lasting years.

19:27 Three US tribes inside the military were incompatible
In eastern Afghanistan there were three ‘tribes’ within the US military: conventional forces; the Green Berets (working with local partners such as training Afghan National Army commandos and local police); and the Joint Special Operations Task Force (such as Task Force 373, made up mainly of SEAL Team Six and Rangers, conducting night raids). The three had different goals and sometimes supported each other, but more often got in each other's way. The task force might kill someone conventional forces could have easily arrested, while in remote areas conventional forces could not reach, only the task force could operate. That incoordination was a core problem of the Afghanistan war.

24:56 Commanders measured success with the wrong metrics
Many commanders lacked real understanding of counterinsurgency and could only lean on quantifiable performance metrics: ordnance dropped, miles of road built, number of meetings held. The book gives an example: 2nd Battalion, 503rd Infantry Regiment, fought in Kunar Province for 15 months and lost 24 soldiers, while its commander, Lt. Col. Bill Ostland, defined success by the number of JDAMs dropped, ammunition expended, SERP budget spent and 10,000 Beanie Babies handed out — metrics that could not reflect actual effects and were even self-contradictory.

40:00 Navy admirals with ground-combat résumés
Wesley Morgan points out that many current senior US Navy and Air Force generals and admirals have a chapter in their résumés utterly unlike the standard career path: they led Provincial Reconstruction Teams (PRTs) in Afghanistan's Kunar and Nuristan provinces — submarine officers, nuclear engineers, naval aviators. For example, the current commander of INDOPACOM, Sam Paparo, led the Nuristan PRT for a year. Those assignments coincided with the fighting at Wana and Narisan, and they went out daily in MRAPs on counterinsurgency missions. That experience became a unique mark on their careers.

43:18 Military-media relations went from transparent to hostile
Morgan recalls that in 2007, as a 19-year-old freelance journalist, he could almost freely choose which unit to embed with, and public affairs just helped him reach company- and platoon-level units. But today, since the embed system ended in 2013-2014, relations between the military and the media have deteriorated sharply, and a new generation of officers at battalion level and below sees the media as something terrifying. He argues the turning point was not the McChrystal affair but after Obama's second term, when the military began restricting embeds and pushing the war out of sight, because the complicated message that ‘advisors’ were really ‘combat advisors’ was unwelcome.

57:52 How Multicam became a badge of the elite
Morgan tells the story of how Multicam spread: it was invented around 2002 by a Brooklyn art-school graduate, lost the Army's camouflage competition (the Army chose the poorly performing ACU pattern), but Delta Force adopted Multicam privately because ACU performed badly at night. It then spread through special operations and became a badge of the elite. Crucially, Crye hinted to game producers that this was elite camouflage, so Multicam appeared in games like Ghost Recon before real photographs did, building an elite image in the minds of young soldiers.

item.title: Kent State Shootings: Why the National Guard Opened Fire on Students
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-05-extracredits-肯特州立枪击-国民警卫队为何向学生开火/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-05-extracredits-肯特州立枪击-国民警卫队为何向学生开火/
item.description: In 1970 at Kent State University, the National Guard opened fire on protesting students, killing 4. Confused orders, outdated tactics and an armed standoff turned a peaceful protest into a bloodbath.
item.content:encoded:
In 1970 at Kent State University, the National Guard opened fire on protesting students, killing 4. Confused orders, outdated tactics and an armed standoff turned a peaceful protest into a bloodbath.

This episode reconstructs the full course of the Kent State shootings, revealing the chaos and misjudgment behind the event, and it directly helps in understanding the social fractures in America in the 1960s and 70s.

1:05 The National Guard enters campus under arms
On May 3, 1970, 850 National Guardsmen carrying M1 rifles, bayonets and tear gas entered Kent State University, stationed at the football field and guarding the ROTC building. This deployment enraged students; even those who had not been involved in the protests felt the war had come to their doorstep. But students were not especially afraid, because previously the Guard had usually only used tear gas or brawled when handling demonstrations, and had never shot and killed anyone. This time, however, unusually, the troops carried live ammunition.

3:08 Orders are confused, and the governor pours fuel on the fire
Governor Rhodes's speech was full of inflammatory rhetoric, comparing the protesters to Nazi Brownshirts and the Ku Klux Klan and calling them "the worst people in America." But in fact, his order to formally deploy the Guard did not come until May 5, while the troops had already arrived on May 3. There were serious disagreements among the university president, local government and the governor over the Guard's mission: the president believed assemblies had been banned, but protest leaders and professors pointed out the ban had not yet taken effect. This confused transmission of information laid the groundwork for the later clash.

5:09 A rule changed at the last minute triggers a standoff
On the evening of May 3, students gathered in the plaza to protest, but local government abruptly moved the curfew from 1 a.m. to 9 p.m. and sent police to disperse them. Students saw this as "changing the rules midway," so they split into two groups: one went to the president's house to demand First Amendment rights and was driven back with tear gas; the other sat down on the main road, blocking traffic and singing "Give Peace a Chance." Police and the Guard surrounded them, with helicopters circling overhead. In the end, the Guard used tear gas and bayonets to drive the students back to their dormitories, leaving at least two students stabbed and 68 arrested.

9:11 May 4: a peaceful assembly forms again
At 11 a.m. on May 4, about 2,000 students gathered in the plaza again. Although there was no official state of emergency, university officials still handed out leaflets saying the assembly was illegal. Guard commander General Canterbury insisted the demonstration was illegal, but students still spread word of the gathering through loudspeakers. By noon the assembly was largely peaceful, with only some crude slogans. University police announced through loudspeakers that the assembly was illegal and demanded dispersal, but their voices were drowned out, and a few rocks flew toward vehicles. Canterbury then ordered two rounds of tear gas, but they missed, and the wind blew the gas away instead.

12:13 13 seconds of firing, 67 bullets
The Guard advanced to clear the area and succeeded in dispersing most of the protesters, but one group of 52 pushed too far and was trapped in the fenced stadium, pelted with rocks. Ten minutes later they received orders to withdraw and moved toward Taylor Hall. When they reached the top of the hill, 72 Guardsmen turned around, raised their weapons and fired a 13-second volley, 67 bullets in all. Four students died: Jeffrey Miller (20, 265 feet away), Allison Krause (19, 340 feet away), Sandra Scheuer (19, 390 feet away) and William Schroeder (19, 390 feet away). Another 9 were wounded, the nearest 60 feet away and the farthest 750 feet away.

14:16 One photograph changes America
After the shooting there was dead silence, and students stood frozen in place. Fourteen-year-old Mary Ann Vecchio knelt beside Jeffrey Miller's body screaming, and 21-year-old photography student John Filo took the picture, which became an image that shocked the nation. But the conflict did not end; protests spread across the country, followed by the Hard Hat Riot, the Jackson State shootings and other events. The episode stresses that this history is strikingly similar to the present and worth reflecting on.

item.title: She Fought for Women's Rights and Was Executed for Treason
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-05-stuffmissed-她为女权呐喊-却被以叛国罪处死/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-05-stuffmissed-她为女权呐喊-却被以叛国罪处死/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: Olympe de Gouges is known for the Declaration of the Rights of Woman, but she was killed not for her feminist claims — she was killed for opposing the king's execution and attacking Robespierre.
item.content:encoded:
Olympe de Gouges is known for the Declaration of the Rights of Woman, but she was killed not for her feminist claims — she was killed for opposing the king's execution and attacking Robespierre.

To understand women's political position and one individual fate during the French Revolution. History buffs and people following women's-rights issues will be interested.

1:05 The Declaration of the Rights of Woman answers the Declaration of the Rights of Man
Olympe de Gouges is most famous for the 1791 Declaration of the Rights of Woman and the Female Citizen, a direct response to the 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. The original used citoyen; she switched to the feminine form citoyenne, which looks entirely different but sounds similar. Her writing and political activity went far beyond this one pamphlet, and her death sentence was not for calling for women's rights.

6:13 Biographical truth is mixed with novelistic invention
The first English-language biography of de Gouges, Women's Rights in the French Revolution, draws heavily on her epistolary novel Memoirs of Madame de Valmont as factual evidence, but the book is highly fictional. Its protagonist is widely considered a stand-in for herself, while the Marquis de Flaucour represents her possible biological father, the Marquis de Pompignan. This parentage has never been confirmed.

14:19 The Comédie-Française crushed a woman playwright
Zamore et Mirza was written and submitted anonymously in 1784 and accepted the following year, but its performance was long delayed. When de Gouges kept pressing, the theater revoked her admission rights and applied for her arrest. Between 1761 and 1789 the theater accepted only nine plays by women, and she was the only writer treated this way. She later wrote to the Duke of Richelieu, who helped restore her position.

17:28 Slavery became the first abolitionist play
The play finally opened in 1789, but its setting moved from the East Indies to the Caribbean, its characters from Asians to Africans, and its title to Slavery of the Blacks. It is often considered France's first play to explicitly support abolition and to tell the story from the perspective of the enslaved. Abolitionists praised it, while wealthy men with colonial interests hired hecklers to disrupt it, and the actors refused to blacken their skin for the roles.

23:32 The article rewrites all 17 articles one by one
The Declaration of the Rights of Man granted rights to citizens but excluded women, and the 1791 constitution restricted the vote to taxpaying men. De Gouges's Declaration of the Rights of Woman copied the 17-article format and rewrote each article in turn. Where the original's Article 10 guaranteed freedom of speech, for instance, she added that a mother has the right to publicly declare the identity of her child's father. The whole document was dedicated to Marie Antoinette, encouraging her to advance women's rights.

28:39 Defending Louis XVI became the rope around her neck
Despite her revolutionary stance, de Gouges believed constitutional monarchy suited France best and that the king should be a symbol rather than a power. When Louis XVI was tried for treason in 1792, she volunteered to defend him, on the grounds that the monarchy had been abolished and a republic could not try a former king for acts committed while he reigned. Her logic was called strained; the king was executed anyway, and she herself came to be seen as a royalist.

30:43 Federalism got her arrested
In July 1793, de Gouges proposed that France's provinces govern themselves rather than form a unified republic, which was taken as a direct provocation. She underestimated the ferocious political atmosphere of the Terror, and voluntarily brought investigators to her office, thinking her work would prove her loyalty. Instead, her unfinished play France Saved was used as evidence against her for sympathizing with Marie Antoinette. She was ultimately executed on the charge of opposing the republican constitution.

item.title: The World's Largest Electric Aircraft Just Flew: $5 of Electricity, Taking On Regional Aviation
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-04-ycsp-全球最大电动飞机首飞-电费仅5美元-挑战支线航空/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-04-ycsp-全球最大电动飞机首飞-电费仅5美元-挑战支线航空/
item.description: Heart Aerospace's ES-30 electric aircraft takes off on $5 of electricity, with operating costs 48% lower than the old planes it replaces, targeting half of the world's flights under two hours and using hybrid power to solve the backup battery problem.
item.content:encoded:
Heart Aerospace's ES-30 electric aircraft takes off on $5 of electricity, with operating costs 48% lower than the old planes it replaces, targeting half of the world's flights under two hours and using hybrid power to solve the backup battery problem.

This episode shows the seven-year journey from a 3D-printed model to a 100-foot wingspan aircraft, revealing the economics and technical breakthroughs of electric aviation — highly illuminating for listeners focused on clean energy and transportation innovation.

0:00 The electric aircraft's electricity bill is just $5
The world's largest electric aircraft, Heart Aerospace's ES-30, has completed its first flight. It has a 100-foot wingspan and a 25,000-pound takeoff weight, yet takeoff costs only $5 in electricity. Its all-electric range is 125 miles, hybrid range reaches 500 miles, and charging takes about 30 minutes. This marks the viability of electric aviation in the regional market, with operating costs 48% lower than conventional aircraft.

1:30 Electric motors replace jet engines
Heart's aircraft replaces jet engines with electric motors. A motor has only one moving part, no combustion, and almost zero wear, so it is cheaper to produce and more reliable. By contrast, a jet engine has thousands of parts and burns fuel at extremely high temperatures. Electric motors are nearly silent while taxiing and have good torque characteristics, significantly reducing noise and vibration.

3:00 Regional aviation has been ignored by technology
The complexity of jet engines makes the engine cost for a 30-seat and a 70-seat aircraft similar, which pushes airlines toward larger aircraft and longer routes, leaving short regional flights extremely inefficient. Half of the world's flights are under two hours, but existing technology cannot serve this market effectively. Heart is targeting 40-year-old aircraft; the key to regional connectivity is flight cost, not distance.

4:09 From a Swedish air force base to MIT
Anders grew up next to a Swedish air force base, passionate about aircraft, and later pursued a PhD in jet engines at MIT. Twelve years ago, Elon Musk spoke at MIT and said all forms of transportation would become electric — this became his inspiration. He began researching jet engines by day and tinkering with drones by night, and with funding from the Swedish government built a relationship with Nordic airlines, laying the groundwork for his startup.

6:00 At YC: from LOI to physical hardware
At YC, Anders started with a 3D-printed model and letters of intent (LOIs) from airlines including SAS. They first built a 400-kilowatt motor, which attracted a pre-order from United Airlines and in turn more capital. Anders stresses that every fundraise needs substantive progress, ideally something physical you can touch — that is more persuasive than a business plan.

7:00 United came from the spam folder
Heart's first big customer, United Airlines, came from the spam folder. While clearing spam, Clara found the inbound email and invited them to visit. After seeing the electric motor, United understood immediately and placed an order. This shows the importance of showing the physical object directly, and that unconventional channels can bring huge opportunities.

8:00 In-house manufacturing and testing
At its Los Angeles factory, Heart designs and builds most of the aircraft's components itself, including actuators and the fuselage. They choose to make key parts in-house to avoid depending on a single supplier and to accelerate iteration. The whole factory is like one big test bench, where faults can be injected to test that systems still run safely under abnormal conditions.

10:00 Batteries and the hybrid solution
Heart's battery lab tests cells from manufacturers in China, the US and South Korea; the highest energy density so far is 370 Wh/kg, close to the 400 Wh/kg target. To solve the backup battery problem, they use a hybrid system with a simple turboprop engine as backup, adding about 20% to upfront cost but letting the aircraft fly 500 miles and meet safety reserve requirements.
